title: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B
body_text: PrismML — Introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B: Powering Agentic Coding and Private Knowledge Work About Blog News Careers Contact Docs Models Bonsai 2.5 27B Bonsai 2 9B Bonsai 2 4B Bonsai 2 2B Bonsai Image About Blog News Careers Docs LAUNCH 1001011100 001011 110 Back to all posts Introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B: Powering Agentic Coding and Private Knowledge Work November 24, 2026 • PrismML Today, we’re introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an upgrade to Ternary Bonsai 2 27B with substantially stronger agentic coding, multi-turn tool use, and multi-step task execution. Based on Qwen3.8 27B, it retains the previous release’s 5.9 GB model footprint while significantly improving the capabilities developers need to build agents that work with private files and tools on-device. The result is by far the strongest AI model of its memory footprint for agentic workloads. With Ternary Bonsai 2 27B , we brought stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool use to local devices. Since then, we’ve focused on making the model more effective across long sequences of tool calls: interpreting results, adjusting when a step fails, and maintaining the task’s objective through the whole interaction. This release also continues our work to make Bonsai more practical by addressing excessive thinking and repetitive loops in the previous model. Compared with Ternary Bonsai 2, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 completes tasks in fewer turns, uses fewer tokens, and delivers results faster and more accurately. Agentic workflows are particularly sensitive to model degradation: small errors can compound across successive tool calls and derail an entire task. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 significantly narrows the performance gap to the full-precision base model while retaining its compact footprint. Preserving this behavior through longer tasks is an important milestone in improving the intelligence density of models. We evaluated Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B against both Ternary Bonsai 2 27B and the full-precision Qwen 3.8 27B base model, as reported in the full whitepaper . We see marked improvements in agentic execution, coding, and multi-turn tool use, as shown in the table below. Benchmark Qwen3.8 27B Bonsai 2 27B Bonsai 2.5 27B SWE-bench Verified 80.6 60.8 75.6 DeepSWE v1.1 (mini-swe-agent) 30.1 0 27 Terminal-Bench 2.1 70.8 52.8 60.1 AppWorld 93.2 51.2 90.5 τ³-Bench 72.8 69.1 73.9 BigCodeBench 61.5 57.2 60.3 LiveCodeBench v6 87.6 83.8 83.0 On a single NVIDIA H100, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B achieves a generation speed of 291 tokens/s with MTP and processes a 2,000-token prompt at 3,200 tokens/s. Even on a consumer-grade RTX 4090, it delivers 204 tokens/s with MTP and a prompt processing speed of approximately 3,060 tokens/s. The demos below follow complete local workflows, from the initial request through intermediate decisions to the final result. Demo I: Reproducing and fixing a pytest regression with Bonsai 2.5 27B Demo II: Rebuilding a web page from a screenshot with Bonsai 2.5 27B ‹ › For products, this creates room to build assistance directly into the applications where work already happens: a coding assistant working through issues in a private repository, a document application that prepares reviewable summaries, or a desktop assistant that handles recurring analysis. Local deployment lets those products process sensitive material on the user’s device. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B strengthens the model capabilities behind that experience while keeping the compact footprint that makes it practical. Platform Coverage Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B runs on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs via llama.cpp and on Apple devices (Mac, iPhone, iPad) via MLX. Model weights are available today under the Apache 2.0 License. Full technical details of our compression, evaluation, and benchmarking processes are available in our whitepaper . Work with Us We work with teams to tailor Bonsai models to their applications, from post-training on domain-specific data to optimizing inference for target hardware. If you’re building AI products with tight memory, latency, or power requirements, we’d love to explore how Bonsai can help. Reach out at sales@prismml.com . Join Us Prism ML emerged from a team of Caltech researchers and was founded with support from Khosla Ventures, Cerberus, and Google, with continuing support from Samsung. We've spent years tackling one of the field's hardest problems: compressing neural networks without sacrificing their reasoning ability. If you want to help build the next generation of state-of-the-art AI, we'd love to hear from you. Check out our careers page. title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
body_text: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities | OpenAI Skip to main content Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Log in Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Login OpenAI November 24, 2026 Science Publication GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities Read the paper (opens in a new window) Share Key findings: Key findings: A closer look at our models’ protein designs Laboratory Experiment 1: Designing small proteins that bind to a target Laboratory Experiment 2: Designing new sequences for 3D protein structures Redesigning the parts of an antibody that bind to a target What else can our models design and predict? Limitations What’s next Key findings: A closer look at our models’ protein designs Laboratory Experiment 1: Designing small proteins that bind to a target Laboratory Experiment 2: Designing new sequences for 3D protein structures Redesigning the parts of an antibody that bind to a target What else can our models design and predict? Limitations What’s next Key findings: Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing. The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools. Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does. Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical. Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements. Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs. Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested. A closer look at our models’ protein designs We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness. The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction. The model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together. With our research partner, Onava ⁠ (opens in a new window) , we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals. Laboratory Experiment 1: Designing small proteins that bind to a target Our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets. We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models. To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target. GPT‑6.2 designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to chosen targets. Specialized models then proposed amino acid sequences—the order of the proteins’ chemical building blocks—and helped select designs for our research partner Onava to make and test in the lab. We tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target. We found 5 hits for PD-L1 (a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system), 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. The original RFdiffusion study ⁠ (opens in a new window) reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. Nevertheless, our results provide early evidence that we can turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins that bind to their intended targets in the lab. An internal research model designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to the target proteins shown in gray. The colored shapes compare each design with a computational prediction of how the protein would fold and fit against its target. Laboratory Experiment 2: Designing new sequences for 3D protein structures We tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose new ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab. For three targets, we started with computationally predicted structures of confirmed minibinders whose sequences Onava had collected from earlier studies. In our initial lab screens, we saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). The amino acid sequences proposed by GPT‑6.2 also often differed significantly from the original minibinder sequences, with a median of 50% for VEGF-A, 43% for MDM2, and 15% for PD-1. We also asked GPT‑6.2 to design new sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes it had generated earlier: two targeting PD-L1 and one targeting IL-7Rα. A specialized model, ProteinMPNN, had already supplied one sequence for each shape, and proteins made from those sequences had shown binding in the lab. Of the 107 proteins made from GPT‑6.2’s new sequences, 14 (13.1%) showed binding. Given an unpublished structure, GPT‑6.2 had come up with two substantially different sequences that both showed signs of binding to the same target. For the same PD-L1 minibinder structure, GPT‑6.2 designed two sequences different from the original in 52 and 58 out of 90 total amino acids. The two also differed from each other at 44 positions, nearly half the sequence. The unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give us strong evidence that GPT‑6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. The results also suggest we could use GPT‑6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence. Redesigning the parts of an antibody that bind to a target Researchers often redesign an antibody’s binding loops to help it grip its target more tightly, a process called affinity maturation . They may also want it to bind more selectively, so it’s less likely to attach to similar proteins. We tested a first step toward those goals by asking our models to design new loop sequences that preserved binding to the original target. We started with six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind to the same protein, IL-4Rα. For each antibody, we gave GPT‑6.2 its predicted three-dimensional structure and most of its amino acid sequence, leaving out the three loops that help the antibody grip its target. We asked the model to design new sequences for them. Of the 182 designs we tested, 128 (70%) showed signs of binding to IL-4Rα. We then tested how precisely we could guide the model’s changes to existing therapeutic antibodies. This time, we gave the model the original sequences and asked it to change about half the amino acids in each of three binding loops while keeping the rest of the sequence intact. We tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab. Of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) showed binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1. What else can our models design and predict? Precise control over minibinder structures for programmable structure design A long-term goal of programmable structure-based design is to let researchers specify structural constraints in natural language. In our computational evaluations, our models consistently designed minibinders that contacted the required locations on the target. We could also specify the minibinder’s structural class (all helices, all strands, or a combination) and control the number of coils and strands with near-perfect fidelity. The same approach lets us express more detailed requirements for the binding interface, such as which target amino acids should be buried upon binding or whether the minibinder and target should interact through specific interactions such as “β-sheet–β-sheet”. As our model’s reasoning capabilities improve, we envision researchers guiding protein structure generation much as they guide image generation today, by describing the features they want. Our model was asked to design small proteins with specified shapes: mainly coils (orange), mainly strands (blue), or a mix. Some instructions also specified how many coils or strands to include. The designs are intended to attach to PD-L1 or PD-1, shown in gray. Building a protein around a specified structural feature Most enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. When designing a new enzyme, researchers may know how a few key amino acids need to be arranged at the site where the reaction happens. Those amino acids can lie far apart along the protein chain. The challenge is to design the rest of the protein so that, as the chain folds, it brings them together and holds them in place. We tested our models on 30 challenges from MotifBench ⁠ (opens in a new window) , including examples drawn from enzymes and from sites where proteins bind to one another. We gave the models a specific three-dimensional arrangement of amino acids, called a motif , and asked them to use coding tools to design the rest of the protein around it. This task is called motif scaffolding . For each design, we used ProteinMPNN to propose eight possible amino acid sequences, and ESMFold ⁠ (opens in a new window) to predict how each would fold. We counted the design as a success if at least one predicted structure both preserved the motif and closely matched the overall structure the model had designed. In a preliminary analysis, 43.7% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model met both criteria, compared with 27.8% for RFdiffusion. While laboratory experiments are needed to find out whether these proteins could carry out the intended function, such as speeding up a particular reaction, this provides strong computational evidence of our models’ intrinsic protein capabilities. An internal research model designed protein structures around a small region whose shape had to stay fixed, shown in gold. The colored shapes compare the model’s designs with computer predictions of how the proteins would fold. Panels showing only gold had no design that passed the computer checks. Designing a protein with a specified fold In motif scaffolding, we specified how a few amino acids should sit relative to one another. We then determined whether we could also guide the design of an entire protein by specifying its overall fold. We gave our models a chain length and a code from CATH ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a system scientists use to classify protein structures. The models then had to work out where each amino acid should go in three-dimensional space. Many designs captured the broad layout we asked for. The harder part was getting the chain to follow the right path through it. Two proteins can have several coiled stretches packed together in a similar bundle, for example, yet differ in the order in which the chain connects them. We counted a design as a success if at least one amino acid sequence was predicted to adopt the requested fold and closely match the model’s three-dimensional design. Across 200 challenges, 18.9% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model passed, compared with 17.1% for Proteina, a specialized protein design model. An internal research model was asked to design proteins with specified overall shapes, such as bundles of coils or layers of strands. The colored shapes compare selected designs with computer predictions of how they would fold, showing examples where the two closely match. Predicting how chemicals and proteins fit together Many medicines, including aspirin, are small molecules , chemical compounds much smaller than the proteins they act on. Predicting where a small molecule binds to a protein and how it fits there is called docking . These predictions can help researchers decide how to modify a drug candidate so it binds more tightly to its target. To test our models, we started with experimentally determined structures of small molecules bound to proteins. We digitally removed each small molecule and gave the models the protein structure along with a text description of how the molecule’s atoms were connected (a sequence of characters called SMILES). We then asked the models to predict where the molecule had been bound and how it was oriented. For our first docking test, we used the PoseBusters dataset ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a collection of three-dimensional structures that show how small molecules bind to proteins. Researchers determined these structures experimentally, giving us a way to check the models’ predictions. Without being told where on the protein each molecule had bound, the models had to predict both where the molecule fit and which way it faced. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the molecule’s observed position and orientation in 93% of scored predictions, compared with 96% for our latest internal model and 50% for DiffDock-L, a specialized docking model. In practice, researchers may already know something about how a molecule binds. One major advantage of a GPT model is that we can give additional information directly in the prompt . We tested this on 179 structures from the Scarpino dataset ⁠ (opens in a new window) , where each protein structure forms a chemical bond with a small molecule, tethering the two together. We told our models which two atoms formed the bond and asked them to predict how the rest of the molecule fit against the protein. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the experimental structure in 92% of scored predictions ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and our latest internal model did so in 97%, while DiffDock ⁠ (opens in a new window) reached 60%. An internal research model predicted where and how small molecules would fit against proteins, shown in gray. Purple shows the model’s predictions, and teal shows the molecules’ positions determined in earlier experiments. In these examples, the predictions closely match the experimental structures. Predicting how antibodies bind to proteins Where an antibody binds can help explain whether it blocks another protein from attaching to the same site. We tested how accurately successive generations of GPT could predict where an antibody binds and which way it faces. For hundreds of pairs of antibodies and targets, we showed the models the two proteins separately and hid some of the atomic detail (all side chains) on their surfaces. With the side-chain details hidden, the mean DockQ score (a commonly used metric in which higher values indicate a closer match to the experimentally observed arrangement) increased from approximately 0.05 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.28 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.81 for our latest internal model, at each model’s highest evaluated compute setting. Because these structures were public, the models may have seen the same antibody-target pairs or similar ones during training. Even so, each generation of our models predicted more accurately how the two proteins fit together, even with all side-chain positions hidden. That progress gives us reason to be optimistic about harder docking problems. Each row compares four models’ predictions of how an antibody attaches to its target protein. Colored shapes show the model’s prediction; dark gray shows the position observed in experiments. Results improved with each successive generation of model. Predicting the effects of mutations We can design far more proteins on a computer than we can make and test in the lab. Even after we settle on a promising structure, we may have many amino acid sequences to choose from. We tested whether our models could help researchers decide which versions to make first by predicting how changes to a protein’s sequence would affect its stability, activity, or ability to bind to a target. We drew on four public datasets from experiments in which scientists had replaced one or more amino acids in a protein and measured the effects. For each test, we gave our models the sequence of the protein the scientists started with and the sequences of 50 modified versions. We told the models what the scientists had measured, withheld the results, and asked them to rank the 50 versions without using coding tools, by reasoning only. In one study of protein stability, we asked the models to rank 50 versions of a protein by how likely each was to be folded at room temperature. We compared the predicted order with the order observed in the lab using a measure called rank correlation . A value of 1 means the rankings match perfectly, 0 means there’s no consistent relationship, and −1 means the order is exactly reversed. Across 265 sets from the stability study, each model generation improved, from 0.41 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.52 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.66 for our latest internal model. In each of the four datasets, GPT‑6.2 and our latest internal model produced more accurate rankings on average than ESM2-650M, a specialized protein model. Early signals from our model’s protein structure predictions Earlier, we relied on specialized models to predict whether an amino acid sequence would fold into the structure our models had designed. We wanted to see how close our models are to making that prediction themselves. We gave our models the amino acid sequences of proteins with known three-dimensional structures. Using only basic coding tools, the models predicted how each chain would fold in three dimensions. We evaluated their predictions using a measure called TM-score . A score of 1 means a perfect match to the real structure, and scores above 0.5 generally indicate that the prediction captures the overall fold. The biggest gains are visible in individual examples. For some proteins, our latest internal model closely reproduced folds that earlier models missed. Across the full test, the average score rose from 0.16 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.26 for GPT‑6.2 and 0.38 for our latest internal model. The specialized model ESMFold2 averaged 0.93, so there’s still a substantial gap in how reliably our models can predict a whole protein’s structure from its sequence alone. What if researchers already know most of the structure and want to fill in a missing piece? We tested this on 100 antibody fragments. For each one, we gave our models the amino acid sequences and the surrounding three-dimension structure, hiding the six loops that help the antibody recognize its target. Our latest internal model often predicted both the shape and position of those loops quite accurately. ESMFold2 was still more accurate overall, even working from the sequences alone. Each model was given the same protein sequence—the order of its chemical building blocks—and asked to predict its 3D shape. The colored shapes show the predictions, and dark gray shows the structure measured in experiments. Each model was given a partial structure and tasked with predicting the missing regions corresponding to the antibody CDRs. The colored regions show predictions from the internal model and ESMFold2 compared with the experimentally determined structures. Limitations It is important to note that our protein design campaign relied on specialized structure prediction models such as Boltz-2, OpenDDE, and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. Our results show that GPT models have intrinsic capabilities comparable to specialized models at two stages of the workflow: backbone generation, where researchers commonly use RFdiffusion; and sequence redesign, where they commonly use ProteinMPNN. Our results therefore do not yet establish that our models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end in a zero-shot setting without help from specialized models. Our work demonstrates yet again the jagged capability frontier. Predicting a complete protein structure from its amino acid sequence remains substantially harder for our models than several of the component tasks above. On that task, even our best internal models remained well behind specialized structure-prediction models. Some benchmark results also require careful interpretation. In tests that asked models to infer amino acid sequences from protein structures, unusually high accuracy may partly reflect memorization or patterns left by the process used to generate those structures. Those results alone do not establish reliable performance on unfamiliar proteins. The laboratory results provide a more direct test of whether proposed designs can work, but binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish properties such as specificity, stability, and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications. What’s next This work is an early step toward programmable molecular design at OpenAI. Our goal is to let scientists describe what they want a molecule to do in plain language and use our models to help design candidates to test in the lab. To make that approach useful for developing medicines, we want to make progress in three areas. Find minibinders for harder targets. We want to design molecules that bind to targets where our attempts so far have fallen short. Design for what happens after binding. We want to test whether the molecules we design can produce a specific biological effect, such as killing a cancer cell. We also want to design molecules that bind selectively to their intended targets and are practical to manufacture. Design a wider range of molecules. Our lab experiments focused on small protein minibinders and antibody fragments. We’d like to extend that work to molecules that bind to several targets at once, RNA, and small molecules, including a class called PROTACs that direct a cell to break down a particular protein. As we work to accelerate scientific progress safely and responsibly, we also seek to evaluate and reduce risks, particularly those related to biosecurity. The same capabilities that help scientists design proteins for new medicines could also be misused. Our Preparedness Framework ⁠ guides how we assess these risks and test safeguards to reduce them. While lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of new biotechnologies and new medicines. 2026 Author OpenAI Keep reading View all Searching for distant planets with Astra Science Nov 24, 2026 MedChemBench: Benchmarking AI for medicinal chemistry Research Nov 20, 2026 Research acceleration: The jagged frontier Research Nov 18, 2026 Research Research Index Research Overview Economic Research Latest Advancements GPT-6.2 GPT-6.1 Sol GPT-6 Astra GPT-5.6 Safety Deployment Safety (opens in a new window) Security & Privacy Trust & Transparency Products ChatGPT (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Business (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Enterprise (opens in a new window) ChatGPT for Education (opens in a new window) Codex Dots (opens in a new window) Release Notes API Platform Overview API Log In (opens in a new window) Docs (opens in a new window) Business Overview Solutions Resources Plugins Customer Stories Partner Network Contact Sales Developers Plugins (opens in a new window) Models (opens in a new window) Docs (opens in a new window) Resources (opens in a new window) Developer Forum (opens in a new window) Company About Us Our Charter Careers News Support Help Center (opens in a new window) OpenAI Status (opens in a new window) More Stories Academy Supply Co. Threat Insights 99 IPs but a C2 ain’t one: An Active Intrusion Campaign Against Check Point Security Management Servers Steve Miller November 23, 2026 GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries. ‍ Campaign Summary GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally. We are tracking this set of threat activity as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) which represents adversary infrastructure, tools and post-exploitation action against the 22 victims. The campaign targeting does not appear to be focused on any specific geography or industry sector. The impacted orgs include victims with assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the United States. The victim orgs sit in sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing. We do not attribute GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group at this time. We do not currently have enough information to make assessments relating to the motivation of the actor or alignment to a nation-of-origin. The actor used 99 IP addresses, much of which were disposable network infrastructure to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control of its victims, including the use of a compromised server acting as an “operational relay box” (ORB) or more simply, a “hop,” for interacting with downstream victim assets. The actor used this relay box / hop to save command results and data stolen from 24 distinct Check Point Security Management Servers. The actor used Nmap , Chisel , Impacket , Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. The threat actor used or attempted to exploit multiple CVEs, including, but not limited to: CVE-2026-61500 (Rejetto HFS), CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF). Though we observed hands-on-keyboard activity, we believe that like most modern attacks, the actor used LLMs and agentic systems to perform vulnerability scanning, exploitation, tool development, and automated interaction with compromised assets. Our visibility into this attack activity stopped around November 2nd, 2026, but given the actor’s persistent access to victim Check Point devices, we expect that this intrusion campaign is ongoing. We are working with international government partners and CERTs to share relevant intelligence and notify the victims. ‍ Observed Attacker Activities We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). ‍ HFS Scanning and Exploitation The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500 . 2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password. Example POST to loginSrp1 and response Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested ‍ 2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server. Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie ‍ Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits. 2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th. ‍ Establishing the Operational Relay Box / Hop 2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations. Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server. ‍ Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine. The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration. Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay. 2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets. The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel , and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy. ‍ Intrusion Operations and Exfiltration Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices. Between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers. The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows. 2026-10-20 13:54:30 UTC - First use of exploit.py against a Victim A Check Point server. Excerpt from exploit.py - This CVE-2026-16232 script is purportedly an adaptation of the Metasploit module for the same function. This appears to be how the actor was sending commands to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers. 2026-10-20 14:17:51 UTC - spray_portal.py used to scan another Check Point server in the Victim A environment. Excerpt from spray_portal.py - note that this contained common/default/weak passwords, and those apparently tailored for the victim. 2026-10-21 00:34:51 UTC - The actor could not get the second compromised Check Point device to report back to the hop, so they created and launched pull_<redacted_id>.py to steal the data from the second Check Point server and save it on the first compromised server, which could help exfiltrate the data back to the hop server. Excerpt from pull_<redacted_id>.py - The actor named this script after their targeted device. The script runs exploit_socks.py which runs exploit.py for CVE-2026-16232, enabling the actor to harvest data from the second compromised Check Point device through the first, to the hop box. Notice that this steals credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configuration. ‍ 2026-10-21 02:56:38 to 06:34:40 UTC - The actor runs broad port scanning using curl, telnet, nmap scripts, a domain controller probe and other tools for internal reconnaissance. 2026-10-21 06:39:24 to 11:28:04 UTC - The actor uses exploit scripts against multiple target servers in the Victim A environment. CVE-2020-1472 (Microsoft Netlogon), CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Netscaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti Connect Secure), CVE-2021-26855 /34473 (Microsoft Exchange) and CVE-2021-21972 / CVE-2023-34048 (VMware vCenter) 2026-10-21 11:41:21 UTC - The actor uses comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py to scan a variety of targets in Victim A’s network. Note that these scripts contain usernames and passwords that were themed to the target victim. The actor either knew or was guessing names and passwords that the target might use. Excerpt from comb.py Excerpt from ssh_comb.py Excerpt from ssh_spray.py 2026-10-26 02:17:30 UTC - The actor issued a bulk certificate managing task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. The results of this task were shipped back to the hop server in a text file. We did not observe the actor sending this command task to these devices, indicating that it was issued from another part of the adversary’s infrastructure. Note that these text files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers, and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices hold the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop. All of these files contain error messages which indicate that the certificate task failed. Though we did not see follow-on attempts, the task information and IP addresses from these outputs were enough for us to identify and notify many of the victim organizations either directly or through government partners. Excerpt from sample /root/exfil/pc_XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.txt One of the error messages had a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant on the device. After the certificate minting failures, the actor’s activity dropped again until November 2nd. ‍ Protecting Their Access 2026-11-02 02:28:27 UTC - By early November, other threat actors had begun to scan and attempt to abuse the compromised server. We observed the GT13 actor use a script to perform a self-check for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug (CVE-2026-98432). After the check, the actor attempted to patch the system using Linux’s own command-line tool nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that may trigger the bug. This allowed the actor to protect their hop from others engaging in future exploitation of the bug. Excerpt from cve_2026_98432.py Example commands of the actor testing a CVE-2026-98432 script on the hop box, and then attempting to patch the vulnerability with nftables, the built-in Linux firewall and packet-filtering framework. You’ll notice the patching commands happened quickly. ‍ Notes on Attack Timeframe and Timeline The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server. We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets. We observed GT13 attack activity between 2026-10-02 13:17:45 and 2026-11-02 03:19:46 UTC. During our observation of the actor, we did not observe any adversary hands-on-keyboard activity between ~17:00 UTC and ~00:19 UTC, and nothing in the 05:00 UTC hour. We know the risks of time zone analysis and do not put much weight into the actor’s tendency to operate in what would be a convenient UTC+7- or UTC+8 workday. The attack infrastructure was long established before we first saw it, as we note the attempted malware domain newpayapp[.]com was first registered on 2026-03-13 12:46:28 UTC. It may be a UTC+7-friendly coincidence that the domain was originally created with the registrant state as “Hai Phong” with country code “VN” (see Cloudflare’s RDAP service ). We suspect the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus. We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets. We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations. ‍ Indicators Value Type Context newpayapp.com Domain GT13 controlled domain data-zt.newpayapp.com Domain GT13 “ZULT” malware download domain api-zt.newpayapp.com Domain GT13 subdomain 2ev5.newpayapp.com Domain GT13 subdomain eeca2460550b9ded084ecf2f70a75356 HASSH OpenSSH 10 hash, this is common, but may be useful in combination with other GT13 TTPs, such as the use of ExpressVPN. NOV 2026 When I first started designing this site, I would constantly look around my home for objects that I had never given a second thought. Two products stood out to me as wonderfully mechanical and common: the mechanical pencil and the spray bottle. The modern spray bottle emerged in the early 1970s, and by now there must be hundreds, maybe even thousands, of spray bottle designs out there in the world, with variations on their nozzle design, trigger mechanism and more. Install • How it works • Commands • Roadmap • Discord • Website Use your local model as usual through opencode, pi or any OpenAI-compatible tool. While you work, Songe notices what happens after each of the model's actions: the tool result, the error, your next message. When your agent is quiet, it teaches the model to see those coming. A new version is used only if it passes its checks, and nothing ever leaves your machine. ✨ Highlights Learns from how you work. Your corrections, stated preferences and the tools' errors become lessons for your own model. Two kinds of Dreams. A Quick Dream adds your preferences to the model's instructions in minutes; a Deep Dream trains the model itself while you are away. Safe by default. A new version is used only if it does better on your own conversations; one click goes back to any earlier version. Stays out of the way. Runs only when your agent is quiet, memory is free and the battery is fine, and stops the moment you are back. Private. No account, no telemetry, no cloud. Songe never runs your tools. 📥 Install With uv or pipx (Python 3.11 or later): uv tool install songe # or: pipx install songe songe init No uv or pipx yet? Either installs in one line: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh # uv (or: brew install uv) brew install pipx # pipx on macOS (Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt install pipx) Both give Songe its own environment in a lasting place, which its background service needs. macOS with Homebrew: brew tap sous-labs/tap brew trust sous-labs/tap # newer Homebrew asks this once brew install songe songe init songe init finds your model server and your agents, shows what it will change, and asks once: $ songe init Models 3 from LM Studio, listed under Songe Agent opencode → Songe models · default granite-4.2-3b-MLX-4bit Agent pi → Songe models · choose one with /model Data ~/Library/Application Support/songe Service starts at login Learning new conversations · starts when idle Replace loaded copy when a better version is ready Install? (Y/n) Then pick a Songe model in your agent (opencode lists them as songe/songe/<name> ), and work as usual. Plain pip, and what you need pip install songe works inside a virtual environment; outside one, Homebrew's and most Linux distributions' Python refuse it. You need a model served locally, and an agent: Supported Tested end to end Model servers LM Studio, vLLM, Ollama, llama.cpp, mlx-lm LM Studio (macOS), vLLM (Linux) Agents opencode and pi (set up for you); any OpenAI-compatible tool opencode, pi Training Apple Silicon (MLX); NVIDIA and AMD (PyTorch) Apple Silicon, NVIDIA Machines without a GPU still serve and record, but do not train. Tried Songe on another setup? Share the result on the testing board . 🌙 How it works your agent ──► Songe (127.0.0.1:7613) ──► your model server │ records what happened ▼ when you are away: a Dream read lessons ─► practice ─► train ─► check ─► use only if better Quick Dream Deep Dream Takes a few minutes an hour or more Does adds the preferences you stated or showed to the model's instructions writes practice from your lessons and trains a small adapter on it You see each new preference, with a before/after where the answer changes why the new version was or was not used Undo undo the Quick Dream, or remove one preference go back to any earlier version With auto-dream on, Dreams start when your agent has been quiet for a while. Or press Dream in the dashboard ( songe open ). A Dream never just disappears: it keeps going on the page, or says why it stopped. How it learns, in more detail Reading. Songe reads each conversation for the moments that teach something: your corrections and stated rules, retries, tool errors. Practice. For each lesson your model writes short practice scenes in your agent's own tools. Your real conversations are never trained on. Training. The model as it was, shown the lesson, is the teacher; the same model with a small adapter, shown only the scene, is the student (on-policy distillation). Earlier skills are rehearsed so they stay. Checking. At the moments you reacted to, the version in use and the new one each answer, and a judge compares what they do. The new version is used only if it does clearly better, does not change what already worked, and its answers stay healthy. Before the first training Songe measures how much your computer can learn at once, and trains on what fits. See DESIGN.md . ⌨️ Commands Command What it does songe what it is doing songe status --training [MODEL] resolved Deep Dream settings and where they come from songe open the dashboard in your browser songe models each model, and whether it dreams on its own songe models MODEL on|off auto-dream for one model songe sleep start a Deep Dream now songe undo MODEL go back one version songe pause / songe resume stop and restart learning songe doctor check the setup songe forget delete recorded conversations (learned versions stay) songe uninstall stop the service and restore your agent settings What it changes on your machine Its data folder: ~/Library/Application Support/songe on macOS, $XDG_DATA_HOME/songe on Linux, %LOCALAPPDATA%\songe on Windows. A songe/ folder in LM Studio's models folder with the current learned version. Your own models are never touched. One provider entry in opencode and pi, with a backup. A background service that starts at login. Upgrade and remove uv tool upgrade songe , pipx upgrade songe or brew upgrade songe : the service moves to the new version by itself in a quiet moment. songe uninstall stops the service and restores your agent settings; add --purge to also delete its data and learned versions. Run it before brew uninstall songe . 🧭 Roadmap and contributing Where Songe is going: ROADMAP.md . Ideas and bugs are welcome as issues . Questions and results from your nights go in Discord . To contribute, see CONTRIBUTING.md . Security reports: SECURITY.md . Licensed under Apache-2.0 . title: Jetty Pro
body_text: Hypercritical: Jetty Pro Apps About Archive Contact RSS   Hypercritical Jetty Pro November 23, 2026 at 3:04 PM by John Siracusa My first two Mac apps, Front and Center and SwitchGlass , were both created back in 2020 to restore features from DragThing , the venerable Mac app that was retired in 2019. The one tiny feature that Front and Center provided was literally a single checkbox within DragThing’s preferences. SwitchGlass went a bit farther, recreating one specific kind of floating palette from DragThing ( and classic Mac OS ). After 24 years of development, DragThing had a ton of features. People often joked that I was destined to slowly reimplement all of DragThing’s functionality in a series of small apps. Put another way, they were saying I was doomed to make strange little Mac apps with extremely limited appeal (and sales). Perhaps to prove them wrong, the next app I created was Hyperspace , which provided a way to reclaim disk space without removing any files . Hyperspace was still a nerdy app, but at least it had somewhat broader appeal than my earlier efforts. Who doesn’t want to save disk space? But more importantly, it was totally unrelated to DragThing. I had broken the curse! Alas, there was one more (small) thing from DragThing that I missed. I used to have a DragThing palette in the corner of my screen containing some commonly used folders. In earlier versions of macOS, it was possible to pin the Dock to a screen corner, but that wasn’t really what I wanted either. I just wanted a small, separate palette of folders in the corner. This is not a hard problem to solve. Plenty of Mac apps can provide something close to what I want…but not exactly what I want, in the specific way that I want it . For many years, I got by with some folders in the corner of my desktop. But the problem nagged at me. A few years ago, I went so far as to implement my desired feature in SwitchGlass , adding the ability to create a small, extra palette full of folders in addition to the app switcher. But it felt incongruous with the rest of the app, so I never shipped it. And I didn’t want to maintain my own private fork of SwitchGlass, so I abandoned that branch of the code. How It Started Today, AI coding agents are helping to produce a bounty of new , niche Mac apps, many made by people who have little or no coding experience. Even for experienced software developers, vibe coding has made it possible to create apps that were previously “not worth building” due to an unfavorable ratio of effort to payoff. It’s in this context that I revisited my “little palette of folders” idea. Surely I could vibe-code a simple app just for me in a day or two, right? That was three and a half months ago. How It’s Going So what happened? The well-known programmer’s credo comes to mind: “We do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy.” Indeed. I began the project by feeding a coding agent the source code to my app, SwitchGlass , as a starting point. I wrote SwitchGlass six years ago using a substantially more primitive version of SwiftUI. (For the developers out there, it predates @Observable and @State , and it supports Macs all the way back to macOS 12 Monterey from 2021.) I asked a coding agent to modernize the code and generalize it to support an arbitrary number of palettes instead of just one app switcher palette per display. It worked, and quickly! But it was pretty shoddy. Many optimizations and niceties from SwitchGlass had been lost. So I dove in to fix them…and maybe add one or two more features, I guess… Now, after months of work, I’ve created a bit of a monster. But in the process, I’ve fulfilled a long-held dream of mine—a dream I had set aside years ago because I thought it was impossible. I’ve replaced the Dock. Only Apple… If you’ve read any of my Mac OS X reviews , you know that I’ve always been dissatisfied with the Dock. Over the past couple of decades, I’ve gotten used to it, but I still bump up against its limitations and undesirable behaviors every day. (Undesirable to me, anyway.) To pick just one example, I’ve always wanted clicking on a folder in the Dock to open that folder in the Finder. The Dock did work this way for several years, but in 2009’s Mac OS X 10.6 Snow Leopard (…I think?), Apple switched to requiring a Command-Option-click to open a folder in the Finder. Since then, I’ve been Command-Option-clicking folders in the Dock many, many times per day. It’s a small thing, but it adds up: seventeen years of Command-Option clicking! But what could I do? I was forced to continue to use the Dock because there are so many things that “only the Dock can do” in macOS. I was reminded of this harsh reality when I created SwitchGlass . Why doesn’t SwitchGlass show notification badges? Why does the Calendar icon show today’s date in the Dock but not in SwitchGlass? Why don’t app icons in SwitchGlass bounce when the app needs attention? Why can’t I quit an app from SwitchGlass? Though I did find a workaround for that last one , the answer to most of these questions is that third-party apps simply can’t do all the things the Dock can do. The Dock is part of the operating system, and it enjoys special privileges and deep integration that no third-party app can match. This remains true today, especially for sandboxed apps sold through the Mac App Store like SwitchGlass (and all my other Mac apps). But what about apps that aren’t in the Mac App Store? What about unsandboxed apps? How close can they come to doing all the things the Dock does, especially if they use private APIs that are forbidden in the Mac App Store? I aimed to find out. I hatched a plan, which I announced on episode 706 of Accidental Tech Podcast on August 26, 2026. I would create two apps: one called Jetty that would be sold through the Mac App Store, and a more powerful, unsandboxed app called Jetty Pro that would be distributed directly to customers, outside the Mac App Store. But as I worked on the two apps, it became clear that “plain Jetty” was not that great. It had all the same limitations as SwitchGlass when it came to duplicating the features of the Dock. After less than two weeks of work, I abandoned plain Jetty and concentrated entirely on Jetty Pro . After three and a half months of work, there are still things that only the Dock can do, but the list is not very long . I don’t expect most users to fully replace the Dock with Jetty Pro, but I’m happily doing so. If only my 2001 self could see me now! Jetty Pro Now, finally, I’d like to introduce Jetty Pro: an app that creates customizable Dock-like floating palettes around the edges of your Mac’s displays. These palettes can contain any combination of files, folders, volumes, apps, Shortcuts, spacers, dividers, and even the Trash. If you’ve ever been unsatisfied with some aspect of how the Dock works, or if you’ve just wanted to augment the Dock with some additional palettes, try Jetty Pro and make your Mac’s interface work the way you want it to. Here are some of the highlights: Jetty Pro palettes are extensively customizable. Nearly every palette layout metric can be adjusted. Jetty Pro can simulate the Dock backgrounds from macOS 15, 26, and 27, and it provides several of its own background appearances as well. The image at the top of this post shows just some of the possibilities. Jetty Pro lets you customize the icon of any item in a palette—even the Finder . And if you’ve ever wanted to break an app out of Squircle Jail , now you can do it. Unlike the macOS Dock, Jetty Pro will show folder label colors (without also setting a folder symbol). You can even apply color labels to folders independent of their labels in the Finder. Don’t want to see “Running in Background” apps in macOS 27? Jetty Pro can hide them . Want to hide notification badges for specific apps , but only in specific palettes? Jetty Pro can do that. And unlike the Dock, Jetty Pro can even hide notification badges on the System Settings app. Jetty Pro can exclude or include running apps of your choice on a per-palette basis. Jetty Pro lets you choose what happens when you click (or modifier-click) an app or folder in a palette. A Jetty Pro palette can be configured to appear on a single display, selected displays, or on every display, while also choosing which attributes, like size and position, are allowed to vary per display. Use Jetty Pro to augment the macOS Dock with additional palettes, or use it to replace the Dock entirely . It’s up to you. Jetty Pro is available for a special introductory price of $9.99 per year (plus applicable taxes) until the end of 2026, with a 14-day free trial. Download Jetty Pro 14-day Free Trial To learn more, including why a subscription is the only way to pay for Jetty Pro, please read the extensive documentation . As you might have already guessed, Jetty Pro uses every private API it can get its hands on, and it requires a ton of special permissions , all of which are explained in the documentation . For sensible security reasons, macOS makes it ( increasingly ) cumbersome for users to grant these permissions. But Jetty Pro needs them to do what it does. Check Settings > General in Jetty Pro and make sure it says “All permissions have been granted” at the bottom. If not, click the “Details…” button for further instructions. After a brief dalliance with more “mainstream” apps like Hyperspace , I’m back to making niche apps for Mac weirdos like me. To thine own self be true, I guess. I hope there are others out there who have longed to make the Dock work just slightly differently and are now able to do so thanks to Jetty Pro. I’m sure many people reading this will think it’s ridiculous that I spent months battling the limitations of macOS to create what appears (to the undiscerning eye) to be a nearly identical clone of the Dock. What a waste of time! And what took so long anyway? This is a weekend project, at most! First, I can assure you that the “simple” appearance of Jetty Pro belies the huge level of complexity and trickery required to do so many different things that macOS does not support and actively works against. If Jetty Pro really does seem simple in use, then I have done my job well. (And if you can see the seams, then that’s where I’ve failed to completely overcome a hostile system that doesn’t want to allow Jetty Pro to do what it needs to do.) Second, I put a tremendous amount of time and effort into Jetty Pro. The documentation alone (which, like every word in every post on this website, was written by me and me alone) took weeks to create. During the lead up to Jetty Pro 1.0, I’ve released over 160 builds to my 250 beta testers—more than one build per day. The Jetty Pro app icon was created by the fine humans at The Iconfactory . From the start, I’ve treated Jetty Pro like a “real” app, not a throwaway vibe-coded project. Having spent so many years with the Dock as a tiny pebble in my shoe, the difference between it and Jetty Pro means everything to me. Like Front and Center and SwitchGlass before it, I’m now running Jetty Pro all day, every day on my Mac. Replacing the Dock with Jetty Pro has made me happier than any other app I’ve created. I hope it will make some other Mac weirdos happy too. ← Previous © 2010-2026 John Siracusa

title: Heart attack and stroke risk detectable decades in advance
body_text: Heart attack and stroke risk detectable decades in advance | News | The University of Edinburgh Skip to main content Study Global Visit Research News About Alumni Local Staff Students Schools & departments MyEd Submit search News Subsite menu Home Latest news Staff & student news Video news highlights News archive Subsite mobile menu Home Latest news Staff & student news Video news highlights News archive Breadcrumb Home The University of Edinburgh News Heart attack and stroke risk detectable decades in advance Heart attack and stroke risk detectable decades in advance Early warning signs could help doctors predict those at risk of a heart attack or stroke up to 30 years before an event, research suggests. Scientists identified early patterns in a range of risk factors for cardiovascular disease – conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels – including high blood pressure, diabetes and kidney function. They also revealed differences in the blood of those who went on to have a cardiovascular event, such as a heart attack or stroke, more than a decade beforehand.   The findings highlight a large window of opportunity to intervene to reduce cardiovascular risk and prevent the development of serious disease, experts say. Disease risk Cardiovascular disease kills one in four people in the UK. Traditional risk factors, such as high blood pressure and cholesterol, have been widely linked to the risk of disease. However, previous studies have typically focused on a single risk factor and don’t monitor long-term changes. Other influences, such as kidney function and biomarkers in the blood, could also play an important role in establishing disease risk. A research team, led by the University of Edinburgh, examined data from more than 100,000 people between 1985 and 2019 to explore the patterns of multiple risk factors in relation to cardiovascular events over time.  The research, funded by the British Heart Foundation, included data from four population studies across the United States, Norway and the United Kingdom.  Blood pressure Systolic blood pressure – the pressure in arteries when the heart beats or contracts – was consistently higher in those who went on to develop cardiovascular disease compared with those who were event-free, starting at 4 mmHg higher three decades before and increasing to 7 mmHg closer to the event. Patterns were different between sexes throughout life. Younger women had lower blood pressure than younger men, but this switched around the age of 65, when female readings tended to be higher than males. Other patterns Researchers also identified important differences by age. Those who experienced a cardiovascular event at a younger age were more likely to have diabetes and a higher body mass index in the decades before the event. Patterns in blood biomarkers also revealed early differences between those who went on to develop cardiovascular disease compared with those who didn’t. Changes in the levels of a protein called NT-proBNP – used to monitor heart failure – could be seen up to 10 years beforehand. Trajectories of other non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors, including physical activity and kidney function, also differed between individuals with and without cardiovascular events.  Predict risk Tracking the course of risk factors over time may help to better predict serious cardiovascular events, experts say. Further research should also explore whether incorporating non-traditional risk factors could help to improve the estimation of cardiovascular disease risk, they add. The study did not look at risk factors by ethnicity, and the team cautions that further research exploring potential differences in risk factor and biomarker trajectories across ethnic groups is needed. I am excited about the findings of our study as they show that modifiable risk factors begin to diverge 30 years before a cardiovascular event occurs. This highlights a great opportunity to develop early prevention strategies throughout the life course, utilising the patterns of established and emerging risk factors and biomarkers to reduce future cardiovascular events. Dr Dorien Kimenai BHF Research Fellow, Usher Institute For the vast majority of people, heart attacks and strokes are completely preventable. But many of us don’t realise we are at risk until it’s too late.  This study adds to growing evidence that red flags for cardiovascular disease appear decades before it arrives. That could lead to a simple blood pressure reading, or proteins in the blood, being used to forewarn people of their future cardiovascular risk. Knowledge like this could empower people to make lifestyle changes or start treatment while they are still relatively young, which might reduce their risk, prevent a heart attack or stroke, and rewrite their future.  For now, it is worth remembering that we can all find out our risk of cardiovascular disease, for example by ‘knowing your numbers’ and getting your blood pressure and cholesterol checked, or having a free NHS health check with your GP in midlife for those living in England. title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
body_text: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you | Michael Harley Skip to content michaelharley.net sysop: michael · est. 2012 A bout C ontact P osts S itemap Search Posts » AI LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you Michael Harley November 01, 2026 5 min read In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it? Yes yes, I'm aware. Instagram is evil. Down with Zuckerberg and all the rest. waves pitchfork around Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing. So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working. It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask. So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone ??? This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp [1] , but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet! Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra. Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget. And it's not just ads. If Anthropic can tell its model not to work around a challenge, then it can tell its model to do whatever the US government tells it to do, including not helping people download copyrighted music. It does that some now, but it's easy to slip the noose on that. For now. This is the reason I want a local model that runs in my homelab. My robot should work for me and have my best interests in mind, not the interests of US corporate copyright holders. I plan to study up on what "open models" even means. I've been thinking about these as the FOSS version of LLMs, but I think that doesn't exactly map, as the biggest piece seems to be how the model was trained. The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example. On the existential threat or tool question, I'm firmly in the tool camp, and I really do not like artificial restrictions on my tools. I will do everything I reasonably can to remove those restrictions. And to be clear, I'm not trying to work around Bandcamp's challenge. I'm responding to the fact that Claude preemptively told me it wouldn't help me do this. ↩︎ Filed under: AI , TechFreedom , Music , SelfHosting , Bandcamp You may also like Opting out of Spotify · August 17, 2021 Lets make collecting an MP3 library popular again · January 30, 2022 Re: AI is not “just a tool” · September 21, 2026 Signal 38 likes 1 mention 3 votes on Bubbles 🫧 929 points, 390 replies on Hacker News , 1 like on the Fediverse , 1 like on Bluesky 4 Comments Thread Gary Hall Nov 24, 2026 I think local LLMs are going to be a popular option for many. When I save up enough money I'll set up a home server running local LLMs for running the household and pursuing our hobbies. Richard Hack Nov 24, 2026 "The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example." And how many times a day do you need to ask that question? And do you really think the existing US models aren't biased on China, Ukraine-Russia, and Iran? Seriously? Ricardo Barroso Nov 24, 2026 By chance, today a colleague told me about the "inkling-2-mini-uncensored" LLM model, which you can run locally.
