title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
body_text: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. Stock skyrockets 31% Skip Navigation Markets Pre-Markets U.S. Markets Currencies Prediction Markets Cryptocurrency Futures & Commodities Bonds Funds & ETFs Business Economy Finance Health & Science Media Real Estate Energy Climate Transportation Investigations Industrials Retail Wealth Sports Life Small Business Investing Personal Finance Fintech Financial Advisors Options Action ETF Street Buffett Archive Earnings Trader Talk Tech Cybersecurity AI Enterprise Internet Media Mobile Social Media CNBC Disruptor 50 Tech Guide Politics & Policy White House Policy Defense Congress Expanding Opportunity Video Latest Video Full Episodes Livestream Live Audio Live TV Schedule CNBC Podcasts CEO Interviews CNBC Documentaries Digital Originals Watchlist Investing Club Trust Portfolio Analysis Trade Alerts Meeting Videos Homestretch Jim's Columns Education Subscribe PRO Pro News Josh Brown Mike Santoli Calls of the Day My Portfolio Livestream Full Episodes Stock Screener Market Forecast Options Investing Chart Investing Subscribe Livestream Menu Make It select USA INTL Livestream Search quotes, news & videos Livestream Watchlist SIGN IN Create free account Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Tech Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. Stock skyrockets 31% Published Mon, Nov 23 2026 8:59 AM EST Updated Mon, Nov 23 2026 4:08 PM EST Ashley Capoot @/in/ashley-capoot/ Seema Mody @SeemaCNBC WATCH LIVE Key Points Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, the board announced in a statement. The Nvidia board said it had input from senior levels of the U.S. government. Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 13 following reports that he engaged in several extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang disclosed one affair in a note to employees. In this article NVDA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 3:21 03:21 Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO Squawk Box Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries. The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk." President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard." Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang. Shares of Nvidia closed up 31% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6. "I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process." Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon Nvidia stock chart. Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said. Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations. Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy." He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." "On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote. Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX , Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected." Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Read more Nvidia news Nvidia shares fall as Huang comeback rally cools AG Blanche, FBI's Patel dodge questions about Huang investigation Congress blasts Nvidia bringing Jensen Huang back Jensen Huang to face Congress the same day as Nvidia GTC What Jensen Huang's return means for Nvidia's Colette Kress Trump: 'I made the deal' to reinstate Nvidia's Huang Nvidia surge: What investors should do with the stock and the AI trade now For weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board said Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it." "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's board chair, Harvey Jones, said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company." Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China. Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls, and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips. "The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., said in a statement Monday. Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set before Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any changes in his plans to testify. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Monday that Huang will publicly testify on Dec. 3 as the sole witness during a hearing titled, "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." "Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., a member of the Banking Committee, wrote in a post on X on Monday. title: GTA 6 Recomp (Leonida) banned from GitHub while lead dev was in school
Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg
body_text: Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg | Farid Zakaria’s Blog Skip to content Farid Zakaria 2026-11-12 · 11 min read Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg Okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features. Can I just add one more? I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs , to make profile-guided optimization reproducible , and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible . But the most fun has been using it to understand performance. Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds. What is the critical path? The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path. A B C D waits E ← critical path extra CPUs run B, C and D concurrently; A → C → E still sets the minimum runtime If you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲 I added a new rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached. 1 1 All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work . Kneel before Zod! Aside: New to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM? Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why? The usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep . 💤💤💤 § Where the time goes Every rewind time starts with two numbers: $ rewind time 7a29e716 libuv-1.51.0 78.0 s elapsed on the VM's one CPU 47.4 s critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs 67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing The first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path : the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before. No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you. The line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis . Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep . A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis : look at where threads block, not only where they compute. On a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤 Here is the whole output for libuv: $ rewind time 7a29e716 libuv-1.51.0 78.0 s elapsed on the VM's one CPU 47.4 s critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs 67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing The critical path by phase 3.54 s configurePhase ██ 1.67 s buildPhase █ 42.0 s checkPhase █████████████████████ 99 ms 5 other phases The critical path by process on path pid process, with what it started 47.4 s 34 init › bash -e source-stdenv.sh default-builder.sh 41.9 s 4076 ├─ make -j8 SHELL=bash-5.3p3/bin/bash VERBOSE=y check 36.4 s 4910 │ ├─ make › bash › lt-run-tests 3.38 s 5412 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime asleep in clock_nanosleep 3.38 s 2.00 s 5013 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept asleep in epoll_pwait 2.00 s 1.62 s 5126 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watch_dir asleep in epoll_pwait 1.62 s 1.60 s 5103 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_close_in_callback fs_event_close_in… asleep in epoll_pwait 1.60 s 1.60 s 5508 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time metrics_idle_time asleep in epoll_pwait 1.00 s, computing 600 ms 1.24 s 6095 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests tcp_write_ready tcp_write_ready 1.14 s 5510 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time_thread metrics_idle_time_t… asleep in epoll_pwait 1.00 s 1.10 s 5132 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_file_current_dir fs_event_wat… asleep in epoll_pwait 1.10 s 22.6 s │ │ └─ 279 more 5.59 s 4077 │ └─ make test/run-tests 2.22 s 4183 │ ├─ gcc -fPIC -fstack-clash-protection -O2 -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE … 2.10 s 4189 │ │ └─ cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c 3.35 s │ └─ 20 more 1.99 s 68 ├─ sh ./autogen.sh 1.99 s │ └─ 9 more 1.67 s 2642 ├─ make -j8 SHELL=bash-5.3p3/bin/bash 1.67 s │ └─ 5 more 1.53 s 403 └─ bash ./configure --disable-static --disable-dependency-tracking… 1.47 s └─ 581 more What would shorten it sooner pid if this took no time 36.1 s every lt-run-tests, 600 processes 6.66 s every cc1, 283 processes 3.38 s 5412 75 sleeps in clock_nanosleep: lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime 2.00 s 5013 2 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept 1.76 s 4189 cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c 1.62 s 5126 30 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watc… 1.60 s 5103 16 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests fs_event_close_in_callback fs_ev… 1.60 s 5508 lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time metrics_idle_time 1.22 s every perl, 9 processes 1.14 s 5510 lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time_thread metrics_idle_time_thread Look closer rewind time 7a29e716 --in PID one process: its threads, sleeps and waits rewind time 7a29e716 --folded the path for flamegraph.pl or speedscope.app rewind time 7a29e716 --perfetto F every process on a timeline, for ui.perfetto.dev The second table is the path as a tree of processes based on Gregg’s colony graph idea. Each line is a process with everything it started, and its time on the critical path. 2 2 A ps snapshot might miss short-lived process invocations; the recording has every fork, regardless of how brief. In this build, make check needs 41.9 of the total 47.4 seconds, and 36.4 of that is lt-run-tests , libuv’s test runner. The test runner invokes 287 tests each spending 1-3 seconds. All of those tests are on the path, and the path is a single chain, so the runner ran them one after another. Worse, most of each test is spent asleep, waiting on timers. Drag can be less than time on the path. The last table answers a different question: how much sooner would the run finish if this part took no time? The critical path method calls this drag . For the truly magical part, we can jump to any part of the path and see what was happening, invoke gdb and fork the run at that moment. A profiler hands you a stack, sampled at some moment you can never go back to. Every frame in rewind time is a moment in a recording, and Rewind can replay the run to it. --in looks inside one process, 3 3 It can take a pid, a program or a word of the command line. so let’s dive into the hrtime test that spent 3.38 seconds asleep in clock_nanosleep : $ rewind time 7a29e716 --in hrtime lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime (pid 5412) 3.38 s on the critical path with what it started, 7% of the 47.4 s path 100% asleep (clock_nanosleep 3.38 s), <1% computing What would shorten it sooner pid if this took no time 3.38 s 75 sleeps in clock_nanosleep Look closer rewind where 7a29e716 115894 --pid 5412 the source line the first row's time starts at rewind time 7a29e716 --perfetto F every process on a timeline Since this test spent 100% of its time asleep, the step provided on the last line is where it began. rewind where replays the run to that step and asks gdb where the thread was: $ rewind where 7a29e716 115894 --pid 5412 process 5412 (lt-run-tests), thread 5412, at step 115894 # 2 uv_sleep ( src/unix/core.c:1869 ) 1867 1868 do > 1869 rc = nanosleep ( &timeout, &timeout ) ; 1870 while (rc == -1 && errno == EINTR); 1871 arguments: msec = 45 locals: timeout = {tv_sec = 0, tv_nsec = 45000000} rc = <optimized out> __PRETTY_FUNCTION__ = <error: Cannot access memory at address 0x7fb172519ae8> called from # 3 run_test_hrtime ( test /test-hrtime.c:39 ) called from # 4 __libc_start_call_main ( ../sysdeps/nptl/libc_start_call_main.h:58 ) 🎯 We can see that the test is calling uv_sleep(45) from line 39 of test/test-hrtime.c , and that it is sleeping for 45 milliseconds. It does that 75 times for a total of 3.38 seconds. 4 4 Turns out that the test sleeps on purpose: it is checking how far uv_hrtime moves across a sleep. There is nothing to optimize in this case. As the cherry on top: the run is deterministic, so step 115,894 is the same instruction every time you replay it. You can open rewind gdb at that step and investigate to your heart’s content. The Rewind app’s Time tab shows the same answers. The path becomes a flame graph, colored the way Gregg colors his off-CPU flame graphs : computing is warm, asleep is blue, and a process shades from one to the other by how much of its time it slept. Clicking a frame picks it and moves the playhead there, so the build log, the process tree and the files all show that moment; clicking a process again zooms into it. When you pick a blue frame, the app replays the run to that part’s longest sleep and shows the stack where it slept: Under the stack, Show source opens the source panel at that moment on that thread, and Open gdb here opens gdb in a fork of the run at the sleep: If you’d rather use tools you already know, rewind time can emit the data in their formats: folded stacks for flamegraph.pl and speedscope , or a Perfetto trace for ui.perfetto.dev . The flame graph below is the real flamegraph.pl output: click a frame to zoom in, or open it on its own . § Kneeling at the altar Every idea here predates Rewind. Gregg has been drawing off-CPU and wakeup flame graphs for over a decade, and build systems have reported critical path information potentially even longer. 5 5 Bazel’s critical path analysis is a great example of this, and it has been around for years. I have been inspired by his work since I first dabbled in eBPF , back when flame graphs were new. 🙇 What Rewind adds is the data. Lots of it. Rewind has that data because it can’t replay without it. On a single CPU the only thing that changes from run to run is the scheduler, so every recording already logs every context switch. This changes the economics of performance analysis. On a live machine, you have to trace before the run, and tracing has a cost. You can only trace a few runs, and you have to pick which ones. Rewind traces every run, so you can analyze any of them later, and do so exactly. It has just been a manic fever joy to take ideas I have admired for years, point them at a deterministic VM, and watch them work in ways that are hard or impossible on a normal machine. Please accept rewind time as my offering at the altar of Brendan Gregg. Improve this page Edit @ e5810dd · Text is CC BY-SA · RSS /nix/store/zs832719ryk4mlcxsclg53bb339c0k0a-fzakaria.com

title: How a Mechanical Watch Keeps Time
body_text: How a Mechanical Watch Keeps Time (Interactive 3D) What Everyone Should Know About Mechanical Watches · PART 1 How a Mechanical Watch Keeps Time Piece by piece, in interactive 3D Martin C. Martin Mechanical watches have kept time for 500 years. Many of their core parts were invented even earlier for giant cathedral tower clocks before being shrunk into portable timepieces. This page explains how a modern one works. I personally think it’s fascinating that a well-calibrated, purely mechanical device can keep time with 99.99% accuracy for $100. They also changed the world and look good on your wrist. This web page was partially inspired by Bartosz Ciechanowski’s Mechanical Watch page. You can think of this page as a simpler introduction or background. When you’re finished with this, that page gives more depth. You can drag any of the 3D figures to turn them and see the parts from the side; on a phone, drag sideways. Contents Hairspring Balance Wheel Escapement Ticks and Turns Gears Gear Train Mainspring Hour Hand Recap Hairspring c. 1675 Start with the part that keeps time. In 1675 Christiaan Huygens, a Dutch scientist, invented the hairspring . It is a flat spiral of steel ribbon, finer than a hair. Its outer end is held still, and its inner end is free to turn. Twist the inner end and let go, and the spiral winds and unwinds, back and forth, at a steady rate. In this drawing it swings once every two seconds, and the rest of the watch follows that beat. Why does a spring swing? Think of a diving board. Bend it down, and it pushes back: an elastic restoring force . Let go, and it does not stop at straight. It overshoots, bends the other way, and comes back again: it oscillates . With no friction, it would oscillate forever. A hairspring is a diving board rolled up. The board’s rest shape is a straight line; the hairspring’s is a spiral. Take hold of the slider under the next picture, and drag it to the right. “Bend” becomes “wind”, and “straight” becomes “rest”. Now give the hairspring a twist: drag the slider to wind the spiral away from its rest shape, and let go. It pushes back. It overshoots and swings, just as the board did. This one move is the whole idea of the hairspring. Balance Wheel c. 1364 The hairspring is only half of the timekeeper. The other half is the balance wheel . While most of its mass is around the outside, it is actually fixed to the spring’s inner end. The spring provides the restoring force . The wheel provides the mass and inertia . Why a wheel, and not a disc? Mass at the rim counts most, like a figure skater who spins slower with her arms out. Old balance wheels had screws around the rim, and watchmakers moved them in or out to make the watch run slower or faster. The swing also takes about the same time whether it swings through a big angle or small angle ( isochronism ). That comes from the spring and the mass together, and it is why a watch keeps time even while the watch winds down. A hairspring alone would oscillate far too fast to count. The wheel slows it to a pace that the gears can count. Mass also makes the swing steady. Push an empty playground swing, and it jerks about. Put a child on it and it swings much more gracefully. A heavy wheel carries its own momentum, so a knock to your wrist, or turning it upside down, barely changes its rhythm. How good is it? A well-calibrated mechanical watch, even an everyday Seiko or Citizen, is about 99.99% accurate. A day has 86,400 seconds, so that watch gains or loses about nine seconds a day. I’m not particularly handy with mechanical things. If I tried to build a table it would wobble because things would be off by a few percent. So it kind of blows my mind that, for $100, I can get a simple, everyday, purely mechanical system and tweak it to be 99.99% accurate! Escapement c. 1275 A second hand that just moves back and forth isn’t very useful. We need it to turn one way only. The escapement turns the swing into steps. The escape wheel is being turned by a mechanism we’ll explain soon, so it’s hidden on this diagram. Without something to stop it, it would just turn and turn. The pallet fork stops it. Its two prongs (called stones ) stick in the wheel’s teeth: a tooth lands on a stone, and the wheel stops. Each time the fork rocks, one stone lets a tooth go, and the other stone catches the next tooth. The tooth escapes , and that is where the name comes from. What rocks the fork? The balance does. On its staff is a small impulse jewel , which sits in the notch at the end of the fork. It’s actually a synthetic ruby or sapphire, so it really is a jewel, a precious stone. As the balance swings through the middle, the jewel strikes the fork and flips it one way. On the swing back, it flips it the other way. So, at each swing, the balance lets the wheel take one small step. The step ends when the next tooth lands on a stone, hard enough to make a sound. This is the tick and the tock of a watch. Ticks and Turns Before we go on, something that trips people up until they think it through. How long does the second hand take to go once around the dial? Each tick is one second, and sixty ticks brings it all the way around. So the second hand makes a complete circle once a minute. A hand is named for what it counts, not for how long it takes to make a full 360° turn. Hand A full turn Second hand Once a minute Minute hand Once an hour Hour hand Twice a day Gears Second hand: c. 1670 The escapement gets the escape wheel turning at a precise rate. But the second hand must turn once a minute, and the escape wheel turns faster than that. To convert a faster rotation into a slower one, a watch uses gears: a small gear that meshes with a big one. Must the teeth be the same size? Strictly, the pitch must match: a tooth and its gap on one wheel must be as long as a tooth and its gap on the other. One wheel can have wider teeth than the other, as long as it has narrower gaps. The teeth on the two gears must have the same spacing, so they mesh neatly. Each tooth fits in a gap of the other gear, so the teeth go past each other one for one, and both rims move at the same speed. Four teeth on each gear are colored. Those four teeth are half of the small gear, but only a quarter of the big one. So the small gear turns twice for each turn of the big one: twice the circumference, half the speed. Why does this second hand jump, when mine sweeps? This watch ticks once a second, to make the hairspring slow enough to see. Most real mechanical watches tick five to eight times a second, so their second hands seem to sweep. Now attach the smaller gear (called a pinion ) to the escape wheel. The gears do not spin freely any more: they move on one tick at a time, with the escape wheel. The escapement controls the speed of the whole train of gears. The big gear pushing the small gear (pinion) is the force turning the escape wheel. What turns the big wheel? That’s a mechanism we’ll explain soon. In this watch, the big gear (called the fourth wheel ) turns exactly once a minute: just what the second hand needs! So the second hand goes on the big gear’s axle. It is the first part of the watch that we can read. Gear Train Minute hand: c. 1656 The second hand turns once a minute. The minute hand must turn once an hour: sixty times slower. So we could try the same trick, and have a gear that’s 60 times bigger than the small gear. But there’s a limit to how small you can manufacture the small gear, so the big gear would be huge. And it would have a lot of teeth which adds to the cost. Plus, it would turn the wrong way, counterclockwise, because every gear turns the opposite direction from the one it meshes with. So the watch slows in two stages. The third wheel runs 7½ times slower, and the center wheel runs 8 times slower than that. 7½ times 8 is 60, so the center wheel turns once an hour. Why is this second hand not in the middle? On most watches it is, but that takes more parts. Many older watches had it off center, as this one does: watchmakers call it small seconds . The minute hand goes on the center wheel’s axle ( arbor ), in the middle of the dial. It makes a full turn once an hour. The center wheel pushes the third wheel which pushes the fourth wheel which pushes the escape wheel. Next up, the mechanism that pushes the center wheel and powers the whole watch. Mainspring c. 1430 This is a spiral spring, like the hairspring. But instead of swinging back and forth, it does one slow unwind over a day or two. In the illustration above, it’s at rest. Below, the outer end is held in place. Drag the slider to wind it up. The spring keeps its length, so its coils draw in toward the center. When wound away from its rest shape, the dashed line, it pushes back, as the hairspring does. A tiny one-way ratchet locks the axle ( arbor ) so it can only turn one way. To unwind the mainspring, let go of the outer end by pressing the button. The block is gone, and the outer end swings around until the spring lies on its rest shape again. That fling is the energy that the winding put in. A watch harnesses that force by attaching the spring’s outer end to a toothed drum called the barrel , invented by Jean-Antoine Lépine around 1760. As the mainspring pushes the barrel, the barrel’s teeth drive the gear train we just built. This is the “hidden mechanism” we mentioned earlier. Because the ratchet stops the arbor from turning backwards, the spring has only one way to unwind: by its outer end turning the barrel. Press the button under the figure, and six hours pass in six seconds. The barrel turns once, the minute hand six times, and the coils move back out to the wall. When the spring is completely unwound, the watch stops. Hour Hand Hour hand: c. 1350 The hour hand must turn twice a day. That’s once every twelve hours. Unlike the 60:1, a 12:1 gear is doable. But the hour hand on that wheel’s axle ( arbor ) is off center! And it would run backward (counterclockwise): a pair of meshing gears turn opposite directions. So we use the same two-step trick we used for the minute hand. This time, 3:1 going out and 4:1 coming back. 3:1 × 4:1 = 12:1. The hour hand goes on the hour wheel, in the middle, under the minute hand, attached to a hollow tube (pipe) that slips over the minute hand’s axle. It turns clockwise, twice a day. Recap And that’s how a mechanical watch works! Here’s a recap, retracing our steps in reverse, from the hour hand to the hairspring. The tour plays by itself, like a short film. The time scale in the corner says how much faster than real time each segment runs. The hour hand is driven by a pair of gears totaling 12:1. Source code Third-party licenses

title: 2035 came early
body_text: 2035 came early | Farid Zakaria’s Blog Skip to content Farid Zakaria 2026-11-23 · 5 min read 2035 came early tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire , GL gears , xeyes , a voice , the weather over curl , or Firefox . I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software. Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true. Atwood’s Law Any application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009 I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software. In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev . 1980-01-01T00:00:00+00:00 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.10.5, https://matplotlib.org/ JavaScript the war JavaScript dies trynix, Nov 2026 asm.js GIMP in a tab METAL written in ten days; every browser runs it 2020 to 2025: five years of nothing nobody writes it; everything runs on it Firefox on Linux, in a browser tab C and C++ compile to it at near-native speed desktop programs compiled for the web the browser's VM becomes the OS 1995 2005 2015 2025 2035 One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev . It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package , over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality. I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix . Aside What is unkernel ? It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026. In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately. 1980-01-01T00:00:00+00:00 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.10.5, https://matplotlib.org/ Thu Fri Sat Sun Mon a strip that says what is loading X11 programs network sound downloads on first use GUI windows on the page unkernel ships a Wayland desktop trynix boots on unkernel by default unkernel on npm trynix unkernel The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm , 1 1 With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster. especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload. 2 2 The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell. 1980-01-01T00:00:00+00:00 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.10.5, https://matplotlib.org/ 0.01 0.1 1 10 100 opencode --version python, 3M-iteration sum() python3 -c 'print(1)' jj --version rg --version hello 2x faster 3x faster 5x faster 10x faster 10x faster 32x faster seconds, first run (log scale) qemu-wasm unkernel JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana. Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser. Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland , and they float over the terminal you started them from. GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2. Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser. Network. curl , git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay. 3 3 Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list. The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈 1980-01-01T00:00:00+00:00 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.10.5, https://matplotlib.org/ GIMP Wine X Windows CC asm.js Chrome Cacao CC asm.js Firefox trynix.dev Firefox Wayland Linux WebAssembly trynix Firefox Wayland Linux WebAssembly trynix Firefox Bernhardt's 2035, drawn in 2014 trynix, November 2026 Here is Firefox in trynix , and it loading trynix.dev , and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 4 4 Don’t get too excited: this took over 4 hours. The inner Firefox needed JIT disabled, the middle one ran without GL, and the outer page used a Wisp relay on my laptop since wisp.unkernel.dev cannot reach itself . Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯 2035 came early. Ladybird is now in alpha
body_text: Ladybird is now in alpha - Ladybird Download News Get involved Sponsors FAQ Donate Andreas Kling — Mon, 23 Nov 2026 Ladybird is now in alpha Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux. I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^) Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional. This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that. If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol. Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself! Stay in the loop Monthly updates about Ladybird, straight to your inbox. title: AMD EPYC Zen 6 vs. Zen 1 Performance: 12.1x Geo Mean in Less Than 10 Years
body_text: AMD EPYC Zen 6 vs. Zen 1 Performance: 12.1x Geo Mean In Less Than 10 Years, Up To 133x In AI Review - Phoronix Articles & Reviews News Archive Forums Premium Ad-Free Contact Popular Categories Close Articles & Reviews News Archive Forums Premium Contact Categories Computers Display Drivers Graphics Cards Linux Gaming Memory Motherboards Processors Software Storage Operating Systems Peripherals AMD EPYC Zen 6 vs. Zen 1 Performance: 12.1x Geo Mean In Less Than 10 Years, Up To 133x In AI Written by Michael Larabel in Processors on 23 November 2026 at 11:35 AM EST. Page 1 of 12 . 17 Comments . This month brought the availability of the new EPYC 9006 "Venice" SP7 Zen 6 server processors. We have seen excellent generational gains with the likes of the EPYC 9686F and EPYC 9996 over Zen 5 Turin CPUs as well as sharply outperforming the competition from Intel and NVIDIA. With the first-generation EPYC "Naples" processors having launched nearly ten years ago, I was curious to quantify AMD's server performance gains over the past decade. So up today is a look at how the EPYC 9996 and EPYC 9686F Zen 6 processors compare to the original EPYC Zen 1 flagship with the EPYC 7601 across real-world workloads for performance as well as power efficiency for some pretty epic gains. The AMD EPYC 7601 launched back in June 2017 as the flagship of the EPYC Naples "Zen 1" processors. The EPYC 7601 was notable for its time with 32 x Zen 1 cores / 64 threads, 2.2GHz base frequency, 3.2GHz max boost frequency, and 64 MB of L3 cache. On the memory side was eight channel DDR4-2666 memory and for connectivity were up to 128 PCIe 3.0 lanes. The TDP of each EPYC 7601 processor is 180 Watts. Now just shy of a decade later, the EPYC 9006 SP7 processors have begun shipping. With the AMD EPYC 9996 256-core flagship are 256 Zen 6C cores / 512 threads per socket, 2.55GHz base clock, 4.1GHz max boost frequency, and an incredible 1024MB of L3 cache. EPYC 9006 SP7 processors support DDR5 RDIMMs or up to MRDIMM-12800 memory at 16 channels. There is also 96 lanes of PCI Express 6.0. The EPYC 9996 has a 600W default power rating. Or for the frequency-optimized flagship is the EPYC 9686F with 96 Zen 5 cores / 192 threads with a 4.05GHz base frequency and up to 5.3GHz maximum boost clock. The EPYC 9686F has a 384MB L3 cache size while also having a 600 Watt default power rating. Over the past ten years of AMD EPYC there has been incredible architectural advancements too not reflected in the key specs alone such as AVX-512 with Zen 4 and further refined in Zen 5, security improvements to reduce the need for software-based security mitigations, and countless other architectural improvements each step of the way from Zen 1 to Zen 6. For comparing EPYC Zen 1 to Zen 6, I dusted off the Dell PowerEdge R7425 server originally provided by AMD for EPYC Naples testing at Phoronix. Nearly ten years later, the Dell PowerEdge server with the dual AMD EPYC 7601 processors still fires up and runs reliably. The AMD EPYC 7601 2P was running with 16 x 32GB DDR4-2666 memory, Samsung SSD 860 SSD storage, and other stock components of this Naples review unit. With the AMD EPYC 9686F 2P and EPYC 9996 2P testing was the Nigeria reference server with 32 x 64GB MRDIMM-12800 memory, and Micron MTFDMBQ7T6THM-1BP1JABDC PCIe Gen6 SSD. The AMD EPYC Naples and EPYC Venice servers were tested on the same software stack with using Ubuntu 26.10 for a very up-to-date open-source software experience. Ubuntu 26.10 ships with the Linux 7.3 kernel and GCC 15.3 compiler by default. In addition to the raw performance testing for EPYC Zen 1 vs. EPYC Zen 6, the CPU power consumption and performance-per-Watt were also compared using the exposed CPU PowerCap/RAPL sensors of 2P processor configuration. 17 Comments   - Quad9 pulled their DNS service from France
body_text: Quad9 Service Deactivation in France | Quad9 Service Service Addresses & Features Threat blocking Privacy Locations Negative Trust Anchors News News Blog Press Media Kit Support Support Setup guides Frequently Asked Questions Search Blocked Domains Get support About About Foundation Council Team Jobs Transparency Report Sponsors Partners PEHR Advisory Council Donate en English Deutsch EspaÃ±ol FranÃ§ais PortuguÃªs IPv4 9.9.9.9 149.112.112.112 IPv6 2620:fe::fe 2620:fe::9 More options Back to Blog November 24, 2026 blog Quad9 Service Deactivation in France ( en franÃ§ais ) Today, November 24 2026, Quad9 will disable services for French users. This means any query reaching any Quad9 service address will be refused, and no DNS resolution will be successful. Our planned deactivation will be at 09:00 Central European (Paris) Time, to try to give users who are unaware a chance to respond quickly instead of having services down outside of normal business hours. We are unhappy to have reached this impasse. For those of you seeing this for the first time, see our announcement of this deactivation from one month ago. The Summary We have received demands from beIn (a sports rightsholder company) to block various domains they claim to be related to piracy streaming sites, so users in France cannot resolve those DNS names. Currently, the courts have upheld beInâs demands, and we have faced fines for non-compliance. We are entirely opposed to piracy, but Quad9 has nothing to do with the piracy sites. This is an attempt to force us to be part of an enforcement regime against third parties. We have a fundamental opposition to using recursive DNS providers as a tool in this or any other content blocking campaign. Putting demands on recursive resolvers has no effect on the origin servers that deliver objectionable content. Attacking recursive resolvers is a futile and counter-productive effort , but that explanation is not understood. The policymakers and courts of France may of course make any determination they wish, even those that seem ineffective or damaging in our view. We wish to remain within legal requirements where it is necessary. We have our own strict views of what we do and what services we deliver. Because there is a mismatch between the case outcome and our mission, we must withdraw from France to remain in compliance with both law and our internal guidelines. This is a terrible outcome, but it imposes the least amount of harm viewed over time longer than the duration of this case. We understand this will cause harm in the short term: users who do not know of our withdrawal will find our services unexpectedly unavailable. Users who have to move to different resolvers will not be protected by our cybersecurity capabilities, and they may choose to use resolvers that are less privacy-focused than Quad9. Repeating the Obvious We object to the core premise of the legal arguments, which is the false assertion that recursive DNS can or should be used as a method to prevent piracy or any other type of content access. Our position is this is not effective or useful, as we have no monopoly on recursive DNS, and anyone can set up their own resolver in just a few seconds (though without the privacy and malicious content protection that Quad9 offers). The courts and plaintiff have not considered this argument and ignore it entirely in the judgement. Their interest is focused on the possibility for us to do what is demanded, even if it has results outside of France, and their interest is not in why that is unjust or unwise or ineffective. So, we will continue to argue with a refutation of our ability to do this accurately without applying French law to all other European nations and the world. How Our Withdrawal Will Work There is an understandable focus on how Quad9 is going to block “French users” when we do not collect user information and have also claimed that geoIP blocking is insufficient for selectively denying resolution for certain names. We understand this seemingly apparent paradox, so we will expand on it as it is a question that is frequently repeated. Our geoIP-based method to identify and deny service to French users is inexact. We are aware that our methods to geographically locate users and declare they are in France is quite imprecise - this is inevitable. By using these methods, we will create conditions of overblocking, where we accidentally classify some queries as being from France when they are not from France, and it will also result in conditions of underblocking, where we do not correctly identify some queries as being from France and inappropriately complete those requests even though the user is in French jurisdiction. This imprecision is a core component of our case: there is no legally accurate way for us to determine what queries are from users located in France versus what queries are from users not in France. But we have no other mechanism - it simply does not exist.Â These geoIP lists are inaccurate in two dimensions: firstly, IP geolocation data are often imprecise or just plain wrong, as IP geolocation is not an exact science. Mobile operators span national boundaries, corporate WANs split networks across nations, IP addresses are bought and sold frequently, and network operators shift allocations across borders. These are just a few of many other examples of how geoIP association may not be accurate. Secondly, IP location does not necessarily equate to user location, geoIP data only is a guess as to the location of the IP address, not the location of the end user. VPNs may exit in France but have the majority of their users in other nations; corporate users in one nation may egress in another due to proxies or internal DNS service distribution - there is nothing about a query that has any indication of the jurisdiction of the origin of the query itself. The data is imprecise, but we do not know to what level it is imprecise. So we must work with what we have. Why Not Block With This Method? We could apply this same geoIP filter database to selectively block French users from reaching the sites we have been told to make unavailable, but this would corrupt our core premise which is that the DNS is not the right mechanism for this blocking to happen. If we comply within France to meet the requirement then we accept the worst eventual outcome for users - we lose our integrity and still do not have legally perfect coverage, plus we will inevitably apply French rulings across borders into other nations. We wish to first remain consistent with our core mission which is to only block cyber risks to end users and not content. Secondarily, we must remain as close to compliance as we can to the legal constraints put upon us.Â By accepting even the smallest of the demands for blocking based on geoIP data, we would admit that such demands are permissible within our mission - that we accept to play a complicit role in aiding companies (or others) to create ineffective and mis-directed regimes of content constraint. We would be admitting that DNS blocking is a valid instrument for the piracy problem - it is not . We would be admitting we will do this for an ever-increasing number of names - we will not . We would be permitting these methods to be applied for more areas of content filtering such as moral, religious, social, or political reasons - we must not . So we accept there will be egregious overblocking/underblocking errors in our blockade of French users but would rather remain steadfast to our stated mission and principles to uphold the integrity of the DNS. We would rather there be a clear distinction made for users of our services: you receive the DNS as you (the user) expect, or if Quad9 is forced to pollute the service with unexpected and arbitrary number of fragmentation demands, then we will not offer the services at all. Doesn’t Quad9 Already Block Names? Quad9 blocks a set of cyber-threats on 9.9.9.9 (and secondary IPs) for end users, where the outcome would be an unexpected and harmful result to the end user (i.e., malicious software). Content blocking is explicitly not in that set. Quad9 has subjective editing on that set, as well - if we believe something is inappropriately categorized by our threat intelligence partners, then we can remove it at our discretion. Additionally, Quad9 also offers 9.9.9.10, which has no blocking of any kind - it is entirely open. The demands we have been given would enforce mandatory restrictions on all our service addresses, which then makes our statements of their functionality inconsistent with the reality that would be forced upon us. We will not accept that condition. The Future Prospects We take a long range and principled view to the outcome of this case and the others in line. There are unmistakable long-term risks to Quad9, to user privacy, and to potential fragmentation of the internet that are far beyond the current moment. To give in now would start âthe beginning of the endâ and allow motion towards internet fragmentation that cannot be undone. We accept the risks and the pain that come with fighting where others in similar circumstances to ourselves must bend and compromise in this invisible card game where end users are not even at the table. We represent those users, and our nonprofit mission of public service is aptly unique by not representing any shareholders, products, or other interests other than the end user.Â It is especially disturbing to us to be doing this for an issue (piracy) which we believe is not slowed at all by any involvement of recursive DNS, though the damage to the integrity and trust of the global namespace is significant. We have seen recent articles about extended blocking demands given to ISPs in France of social media or instant messaging sites, which we anticipate would be demanded of us as well if continued. It is quite clear to us the path that is being taken with these efforts: first create the mechanism, then expand the volumes of the mechanism (unconstrained rightsholder editing of the DNS), then expand the scope of prohibitions to other groups and for other reasons until there is effectively no limit to the number of editors or the reasons for DNS names to be deleted from recursive resolution. This contradicts our mission of delivery of trustworthy DNS results, and we believe this potential outcome to be antithetical to a free and open internet. This is the second legal assault we have faced to see if the DNS can be slowly corrupted - we stood our ground and eventually won in Germany ; with the continued community sponsorship and support we hope to win here, too. We refuse to take even the smallest step towards building the machinery of mandatory DNS restriction, and we will not abandon our obligation to the security, privacy, and integrity we have said we will deliver to users worldwide. We deeply regret having to step back from France and hope we will be able to return some day and offer the same unfiltered services that the rest of the world enjoys.Â Legal battles like this drain time and resources away from building a better, safer internet. Your financial support is what keeps us in the fightâand keeps our services free and open for everyone. If you stand with us, please consider donating or becoming a sponsor today. Close New York State Home Search this website, Open Search Search this website Clear search field Search this website Governor Kathy Hochul Menu Pressroom Accomplishments Schedule Executive Orders Legislation About Contact Send a Message Request a Letter, Certificate, or Citation Request a Proclamation Request an Event Appearance Request a Meeting Consumer Protection November 23, 2026 Albany, NY Money in Your Pockets: Governor Hochul Signs Bill Restricting Exploitative Vehicle Subscription Fees Money in Your Pockets: Governor Hochul Signs Bill Restricting Exploitative Vehicle Subscription Fees S.9348A/A.10411A Prohibits Car Companies from Charging for Built-In Features Amid Rising Consumer Fees, New Law Increases Price Transparency and Puts Money Back in New Yorkers’ Pockets Traducción al español Governor Kathy Hochul today signed a bill restricting motor vehicle manufacturers and dealers from charging consumers subscription fees after they purchase a vehicle. Amid rising consumer prices, the new law guards against a rising trend of car companies charging car owners fees to activate and use built-in features like heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers. “New Yorkers are already struggling with rising prices due to Trump’s affordability crisis, and we’re not going to let harmful business practices increase the cost of living even more,” Governor Hochul said. “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets.” S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model. New York Attorney General Letitia James said, “No one should have to pay recurring fees just to use features in a car they already bought. My office has secured millions of dollars for New Yorkers throughout the state who were charged illegal junk fees when purchasing a car. Unfair fees are fueling rising costs, and I am proud to work with Governor Hochul and the legislature to bring costs down.” State Senator James Skoufis said, “People ought to know they’re able to use their already-installed remote start or heated seats during the winter without a monthly subscription. This new law will simply and clearly prohibit car manufacturers from ripping off New Yorkers who already paid for vehicle features when they purchased their car. It’s a common sense law and I’m grateful for the Governor and Assemblymember Magnarelli for their partnership enacting this legislation." Assemblymember William B. Magnarelli said, "I thank Governor Hochul for recognizing the importance of this legislation, particularly as technology continues to evolve at a rapid pace. This law will help protect New Yorkers from unfair fees and ensure consumers aren’t paying extra for features already built into their vehicles.” The law will take effect in 90 days on February 27, 2027. This new law is the latest in Governor Hochul’s ongoing commitment to help address the cost of living by putting money back in the pockets of New Yorkers statewide. Under Governor Hochul’s leadership, she has: Secured reforms to lower auto insurance premiums for New Yorkers, battling fraud, limiting damages paid out to bad actors, and ensuring consumers, not insurance companies, are prioritized. Signed legislation requiring businesses to notify consumers of upcoming renewals and price changes as well as provide clear instructions on how to cancel subscriptions. Cut middle-class taxes to their lowest rates in 70 years. Tripled the Child Tax Credit , providing families up to $1,000 per child under the age of four and up to $500 for school-aged children, beginning in 2026. Made school meals free for every student, saving families $1,600 per child every year. Sent Inflation Refund checks to 8.2 million New Yorkers — up to $200 for individuals and up to $400 for families. Increased the maximum weekly unemployment benefit by $300 a week. modularity Migration from Exchange and Microsoft 365 Other changes in 1.2.0 Stalwart CLI 2.0 FOSDEM 2027 Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange Nov 23, 2026 - 13 min read Mauro D. Project Maintainer For more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook. Today we are releasing Stalwart 1.2.0, and with it Stalwart becomes a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange . Stalwart now implements the protocols that Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover. Outlook, Apple Mail and the mail apps on phones and tablets connect to Stalwart as they would to an Exchange server, with mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes in one account. Users type their email address and password, Autodiscover does the rest, and they keep working in the client they already know. Exchange support is part of the open source Community edition, under the AGPL. Exchange on premises in 2026 Section titled “Exchange on premises in 2026” Before going into what Stalwart now does, it is worth looking at where self-hosted Exchange stands today, because it explains why so many organisations are looking for a way out. Microsoft has not announced the end of Exchange Server. On paper, on-premises Exchange still exists. In practice, every road Microsoft is building leads to Exchange Online: Exchange 2016 and 2019 are out of support. Both reached end of support on 14 October 2025. Microsoft sold a paid Extended Security Update programme for a while, and according to press reports of an Exchange team statement, it ended in October 2026 with no further extension. Servers still running those versions receive no fixes of any kind. No new features. Exchange Server Subscription Edition (SE) is now the only supported on-premises Exchange, and there will be no more major versions after it. SE does not receive the features developed for the cloud. Even its first cumulative update has slipped from late 2025 to an undetermined date in 2026. The new Outlook does not support it. Microsoft’s own documentation for the new Outlook for Windows says it plainly: “On-premises Exchange accounts aren’t supported.” The APIs are moving to the cloud. New functionality ships only on Microsoft Graph, a cloud API. Exchange Web Services in Exchange Online started being switched off in October 2026 and will be gone entirely in April 2027. None of these steps forces anyone to move on its own. Together, they leave an Exchange administrator with a shrinking set of choices: keep running a server that will not grow, or move the organisation’s mail into Microsoft’s cloud. For many organisations the second option is not acceptable. Email is the record of a company’s contracts, negotiations, legal advice, HR matters and customer data. Placing it with a US provider means placing it within reach of US law, including the CLOUD Act, which allows US authorities to compel American providers to hand over data they control wherever it is stored. Public administrations, healthcare providers, law firms, defence contractors and many European companies cannot accept that, or no longer want to. Data sovereignty means that you decide where your data lives, under which jurisdiction, and who can read it. A mail service in someone else’s cloud cannot offer that, and an on-premises server whose vendor is steering its customers toward that cloud offers less of it every year. Outlook without Exchange Section titled “Outlook without Exchange” The obstacle to leaving Exchange has rarely been the server. It has been the client. Many people have spent their whole working life in Outlook. They have years of muscle memory in it: their folder layout, their rules, their calendar views, their shared mailboxes, the way they book meeting rooms. Many organisations also have workflows built around it, such as delegated calendars managed by an assistant. Replacing Exchange with a standard IMAP and CalDAV server has always meant telling every one of those users to switch to a different mail client, or to reconfigure Outlook into a reduced IMAP mode where calendars and contacts no longer sync. For a migration project, that is often where the plan dies. With Stalwart 1.2.0 the users do not need to change anything. The administrator moves the mailboxes and points the DNS records at Stalwart, and users connect with the same Outlook they used before. Supported protocols and clients Section titled “Supported protocols and clients” Stalwart implements the following Microsoft protocols, all served on the same HTTPS port as JMAP and the WebUI: MAPI over HTTP (EMSMDB and NSPI), the native protocol of classic Outlook for Windows, in both cached and online mode. It covers mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes, incremental synchronisation, the global address list and the offline address book, delegate access, shared mailboxes, rules, junk email settings, reminders, search folders and read receipts. Exchange Web Services , schema versions Exchange 2010 SP2 to Exchange 2016: mail, calendars, contacts, tasks, folders, sharing and delegates, free/busy, inbox rules, out of office, name resolution, distribution lists, and streaming and pull notifications. Exchange ActiveSync 14.1 and 16.1: mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes, with push through Ping, meeting responses, search and out of office. Autodiscover in its POX, SOAP and JSON dialects, so clients configure themselves from an email address and a password. That set of protocols is what the following clients use to talk to an Exchange server, and they can connect to Stalwart the same way: Classic Outlook for Windows (Outlook 2016 and later, including Microsoft 365 Apps), over MAPI over HTTP and EWS. Outlook for Mac , over EWS. Apple Mail, Calendar and Contacts on macOS , through an Exchange account over EWS. Mail, Calendar and Contacts on iPhone and iPad , through an Exchange account over ActiveSync. Android mail apps with Exchange account support, such as Gmail, Samsung Email and Nine, over ActiveSync. Thunderbird , with its built-in Exchange support for mail over EWS, or with TbSync for calendars, contacts and tasks over ActiveSync. Evolution (through evolution-ews) and eM Client , over EWS. Libraries and tools built on EWS or ActiveSync, such as exchangelib. Shared data Section titled “Shared data” The Exchange protocols are not a separate silo inside Stalwart. They are another door into the same accounts. A message filed in Outlook is in the same mailbox an IMAP or JMAP client sees, a meeting accepted on a phone appears in the calendar that CalDAV clients read, and a contact added in Apple Contacts shows up in the CardDAV address book. A user can keep Outlook on the office desktop, the native mail app on a phone and a JMAP webmail in the browser, all on one account. Rules created in Outlook’s Rules and Alerts are stored on the server as mail rules , which run as Sieve when the message is delivered. They apply when Outlook is closed and whatever client the user opens next. Delegates and folder permissions set in Outlook become regular Stalwart shares, so they apply to every protocol. Shared mailboxes open automatically in Outlook from group membership, as they do with Exchange. Not every part of an Exchange deployment has a counterpart. Stalwart does not offer public folders, archive mailboxes, mobile device management, RPC over HTTP (Outlook 2010 and earlier) or NTLM and Kerberos sign-in: clients authenticate with a password, an app password or OAuth. The Exchange documentation covers configuration, DNS and Autodiscover, each family of clients, and the differences from Exchange that administrators should know about before a migration. New Outlook Section titled “New Outlook” One Outlook is missing from the list above: the new Outlook for Windows, the one that Windows now installs by default and that classic Outlook keeps offering through a toggle in its title bar. The new Outlook does not work with Stalwart, and it does not work with any self-hosted server, Exchange included. It is built to work through Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft does not support on-premises Exchange accounts in it at all. The new Outlook does accept IMAP accounts, and that might look like a way around the problem. It is not. When an IMAP account is added to the new Outlook, the connection to the mail server is not made from the user’s computer. As heise and c’t reported in November 2023, the new Outlook sends the IMAP server name, the user name and the password to Microsoft, and Microsoft’s cloud connects to the mail server on the user’s behalf. Every message then passes through Microsoft’s infrastructure on its way to the screen. Microsoft does not only see the mail; it holds the password to the mailbox. For an organisation that runs its own mail server to keep its data under its own control, this defeats the purpose of the whole exercise. We advise against using the new Outlook with any self-hosted email deployment , whether it runs Stalwart or anything else. Users who see the “Try the new Outlook” toggle in classic Outlook should leave it off. The same applies on phones. Outlook for iOS and Android reach on-premises mailboxes through a Microsoft cloud service as well, which requires a hybrid Exchange Online setup. On mobile devices, the native mail, calendar and contacts apps, which connect directly over ActiveSync, are the better choice. Late to the party Section titled “Late to the party” The obvious question is why Stalwart is adding Exchange protocols now. EWS is being removed from Exchange Online, Microsoft’s own future for Outlook is a cloud client, and classic Outlook is reportedly supported until 2029 . Why build support for protocols that will be obsolete in a few years? Because the companies that run Exchange today cannot wait a few years, and because those protocols are the bridge they need to cross. An organisation with a few hundred Outlook users cannot replace its mail server and its mail client in the same weekend. It can replace the server, though, if nobody notices. With Stalwart speaking the Exchange protocols, the server moves first: mailboxes are migrated, DNS records change, and on Monday every user opens the same Outlook and the same phone apps they used on Friday. The organisation’s mail is back under its own control from day one, and no one’s work is interrupted to get there. The client can then change at the pace that suits the users. Over time, as classic Outlook reaches the end of its life and the new Outlook remains tied to Microsoft’s cloud, we expect users to move gradually to third-party email clients built on open standards, and in particular on JMAP . Outlook will stop being an option for anyone who cares about where their email lives, and by then the people who used it will have had the time to choose something else without a deadline over their heads. Exchange support is not where Stalwart is going. It is how organisations get from where they are to where Stalwart is. Footprint and modularity Section titled “Footprint and modularity” Exchange compatibility is not a small piece of work. It adds about 200,000 lines of code to Stalwart, and we know that some of you would rather not carry that weight if you never plan to see an Outlook client. We built it with that in mind, so that it costs as little as possible for those who do not use it, and so that it can be removed cleanly once the Exchange protocols are obsolete: It is a separate module. All of the Exchange code lives in its own crates, behind a single exchange Cargo feature. Build Stalwart without that feature and every line of Exchange code is left out of the binary. The compilation guide shows how. The day the Exchange protocols have no users left, removing them from the codebase is largely a matter of deleting those crates and that feature. It is disabled by default. Even in the official builds, which include the module, the Exchange protocols are off until an administrator enables them . While they are disabled, the server behaves as if they did not exist. It stores nothing until it is used. Outlook and the other Exchange clients keep properties that no standard protocol has a place for: extended properties, reminder state, client settings. Stalwart stores them as metadata attached to the item they belong to, using the JMAP Object Metadata extension, and only writes them when an Exchange client connects and sets them. Accounts that are never opened by an Exchange client carry no Exchange data at all. Its data can be removed. Because the Exchange-specific properties live in that metadata and not in the messages, events and contacts themselves, deleting the metadata removes every trace of them while the items stay intact for IMAP, JMAP, CalDAV and CardDAV clients. Migration from Exchange and Microsoft 365 Section titled “Migration from Exchange and Microsoft 365” A drop-in replacement is only useful if the data can follow. Vandelay , our account import and export tool, migrates mailboxes from both sides of Microsoft’s offering: Exchange Server on premises , through the EWS importer , which reads mail, calendars and contacts. Microsoft 365 (Exchange Online) , through the Microsoft Graph importer , which reads mail, calendars, contacts and OneDrive files. The EWS importer also works against Exchange Online, for as long as Microsoft keeps its EWS endpoint running. Vandelay copies each account into Stalwart over JMAP, and the domain moves to Stalwart when its MX records and client settings change. The migration guide for hosted services walks through the whole process, from the first test account to the cutover. With the Exchange protocols enabled on Stalwart, Outlook and the other Exchange clients then connect through Autodiscover and find the migrated mail, calendars and contacts. Other changes in 1.2.0 Section titled “Other changes in 1.2.0” Exchange support is the headline, but 1.2.0 brings several other features, most of them developed alongside it because an Exchange replacement needs them: Mail rules. Server-side rules in the familiar “when a message matches these conditions, do this” form, managed in the WebUI, over JMAP or from Outlook. Conditions cover senders and recipients, subject and body, headers, size, attachments, importance, message type, mailing lists, spam score, date ranges and weekly schedules. Actions include moving and copying, marking as read or as junk, forwarding, replying with a template and rejecting. Rules are compiled into Sieve together with the vacation response. Each account also gets junk email lists: blocked senders, safe senders and safe recipients. See Mail rules . Read receipts. Message Disposition Notifications ( RFC 8098 ), including the JMAP methods for sending and parsing them ( RFC 9007 ). Working hours. Per-account working hours, managed in the WebUI, over JMAP or through CalDAV. Time outside working hours appears as unavailable in free/busy lookups, and a new setting lets users of the same organisation see each other’s free/busy time without sharing calendars explicitly. See Availability . Rooms and equipment. Resource accounts with a capacity, a location and delegates who manage the calendar, with invitations booked automatically or approved by hand. See Resources . Native FoundationDB client. A new asynchronous Rust client replaces Apple’s libfdb_c library. It needs no client library on the host and is now part of the standard build and Docker image. In our benchmarks it delivers between 4.5 and 6.9 times the throughput of the previous client on point reads, with 5 to 7 times lower median latency and about half the CPU. The changelog lists every change and fix, along with the upgrade steps: existing servers need to add the new permissions to their default roles. Stalwart CLI 2.0 Section titled “Stalwart CLI 2.0” Last week we also released version 2.0.0 of stalwart-cli , and its biggest addition is an interactive console . Run stalwart-cli with no arguments in a terminal and it opens a full-screen interface that covers the same ground as the WebUI: browsing and editing accounts, domains and every other configuration object, watching the dashboard, following live traces and running actions. It is aimed at administrators who live in SSH sessions, or who work on hosts where opening a browser is impractical. The console is built with Ratatui , the excellent Rust library for terminal user interfaces, and it is schema-driven like the rest of the CLI: its screens, forms and field help come from the schema that the server publishes, so it picks up new objects without being updated. The CLI also learned to sign in with the OAuth device flow and to remember the session, so a single approval in the browser is enough for both the console and every subsequent command. FOSDEM 2027 Section titled “FOSDEM 2027” Stalwart will be at FOSDEM 2027 in Brussels. We will have a Stalwart stand, and on Saturday, 30 January 2027, we will give a talk about moving from Microsoft Exchange to Stalwart in the Modern Email devroom. If you are planning a migration away from Exchange, or are curious about what it takes, come and talk to us. We will post the time and title of the talk once the schedule is published. Until then, the Exchange documentation has everything needed to try it, and we would love to hear how your Outlook clients get on with Stalwart.
