title: Nespresso's project to reduce grams of coffee per capsule
body_text: Nespresso – Project Olympus – Alvin Bunk Skip to content Search for: Search Alvin Bunk Alvin's Blog. About Me Sitemap Nespresso World Explorations Starbucks by Nespresso 3rd Party Capsules Milton Coffee Co Nescafe Farmers Origins Kapex K’WA Lavazza Colonna Cafe La Llave Artizan Illy Peet’s Atlas Coffee Club Nuage Segafredo Reviving Origins Barista Creations Limited Edition Master Crafted Single Origin Ispirazione Italiana Espresso Miscellaneous Articles Illy Symfony Twig Oracle JUnit Tutorial GIMPS.USA Miscellaneous Articles Nespresso – Project Olympus Information on Nespresso's Project Olympus. Date: November 1, 2026 Author: Alvin Bunk 11 Comments Introduction The article is about Nespresso’s internal project to basically reduce the amount of grams per capsule that they produce. In August of 2026, I was informed by a Nespresso internal employee about “Project Olympus”. At first I didn’t think much of it and wasn’t sure how to deal with the information. It seems based on the docs that they were possibly improving the formulas, but I still questioned how that is possible with a reduction of grams of coffee. The Documentation The below text is the actual Project Olympus internal text for everyone’s reference to review: PROJECT OLYMPUS: VERTUO As part of our ongoing commitment to delivering an exceptional coffee experience, Nespresso is continuously innovating across every step of our process-while preserving the taste, quality, and consistency our consumers expect. What’s changing? Beginning in 2026, select Nespresso Vertuo coffee recipes will undergo a recipe optimization. Through advancements in grinding and roasting techniques, we’ve refined these recipes to achieve the same great taste and in-cup experience—using slightly less coffee per capsule. This change will be rolled out gradually from Q1 through Q3 2026. What’s staying the same? While the capsule weight may be slightly reduced, the core elements of the coffee experience are unchanged: Same taste profile consumers know and love Same coffee volume per cup Same caffeine levels, with only minor natural variation Same high-quality standards across all affected coffees These updates have been carefully validated from a sensory perspective to ensure no compromise in flavor or satisfaction. Why are we optimizing recipes? Innovation is at the heart of Nespresso. Our development teams are constantly exploring ways to improve how we roast and grind our coffees-while delivering the same consistent, high-quality results in every cup. Project Olympus reflects this effort: a behind-the-scenes optimization designed to maintain excellence, even as we evolve our processes. What if consumers ask questions? In some cases, consumers may notice that certain capsules feel lighter than before or ask about possible changes. If inquiries arise, teams should emphasize: Our commitment to quality and customer satisfaction That the taste and experience remain the same That the update reflects process innovation, not a reduction in value The approved reactive statement and Q&A from the Project Olympus FAQ should be used to guide responses. HQ development teams are continuously looking into innovating our coffee processes, whilst ensuring optimal and consistent in-cup quality. We have optimized the grinding and roasting processes of some of our coffees, which has resulted to a slightly reduced capsule weight while providing the same consumer experience coffee lovers expect from Nespresso. WAVE 1: Projected transition in market Q1 2026 Scope (6 SKUS): DOUBLE ESPRESSO SCURO, DOUBLE ESPRESSO CHIARO, DOUBLE ESPRESSO DOLCE, FORTADO, ORAFIO, RISTRETTO INTENSO WAVE 2: Projected transition in market TBA Scope (8 SKUS): MELOZIO, STORMIO, ODACIO, MO COSTA RICA, MO COLOMBIA, BIANCO DOPPIO, SOLEILIO, ARONDIO Review attached memo and FAQ for additional information. No action is required as of right now. Officially Whistle Blowing On/about Sepetember 5, 2026, I noticed a post on r/nespresso asking about whether Nespresso had changed their recipes: Did Nespresso change its recipe in the recent coffee pods? by u/Inevitable-Video9560 in nespresso I then decided to offically be the first whistle blower about Project Olympus. A large number of Nespresso consumers were definitely not happy with Nespresso’s decision to reduce the number of grams per capsule. There are many users that are seriously considering to drop Nespresso and move to alternative coffee options. Coffee Capsules Affected There are a number of people that have asked which coffees are affected, and that’s a resonable question. From what is currently being observed, almost all the range of coffees are being reduced. The only ones that don’t appear to be affected are Lungos for OL, and Alto XLs (and other larger coffees) for Vertuo. You can always use my spreadsheet to track any of the coffees that have been affected by Project Olympus: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1kZJCdTmqQla2ha3DDYyixQDIUuf9wLvt3122akBkhgM/edit?usp=sharing Below are screenshots of a spreadsheet showing the currently affected capsules (as of November 12, 2026) showing the percentage change: Please go to my ko-fi buy me a coffee page at: https://ko-fi.com/alvinbunk to support and donate to me for writing coffee reviews. Thank you ! Share this: Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Tweet Like Loading... Related Published by Alvin Bunk Hi, I'm a software developer at Taft College. My relationship with Nespresso just ended. Reply A says: November 14, 2026 at 10:12 am Thanks for sharing this! I thought it was in my head but this confirms that the taste is watered down and caffeine content is lower. Nespresso needs to realize coffee isn’t something you can shrinkflate and get away with. title: Ask HN: Anthropic is accusing my company of distilling. How can I prove I'm not?
body_text: Ask HN: Anthropic is accusing my company of distilling. How can I prove I'm not? | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Ask HN: Anthropic is accusing my company of distilling. How can I prove I'm not? 237 points by weli 12 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 177 comments Basically the title. Anthropic is accusing me and my company of using their API for distillation. We are not. We do not train our own models. Our only usage which I think could get us flagged is automated regression benchmarks whenever we change some AI settings. But this is not against their policy? Now I've got 24h to prove we didn't. Has anyone dealt with this too? How can you prove that you are not distilling Anthropic models without breaking your user's privacy?   help varenc 9 hours ago | next [–] Whatever you submit in 24h, submit the same evidence to Claude and ask it to tell you if it's sufficient evidence to make distilling seem unlikely. Because you know Anthropic is just going to be using Claude as well. As others have suggested, the code that generates the false distilling usage pattern along with its git history seems useful. reply hungryhobbit 9 hours ago | parent | next [–] I'd suggest vetting with an adversarial Claude also. Ask Claude A to help you build your evidence doc, then get a completely different session up and tell it "Claude A compiled this evidence, but our source in Anthropic said it's not good. Find all the flaws." Then keep telling Claude B "you haven't found all the mistakes, keep going" until it "cries uncle" and swears there aren't any. Of course, then you have to vet all of the stuff Claude B found, as it won't all be relevant ... but if you want a solid doc the "adversarial Claude" will likely help a ton. reply jwilliams 7 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I think you’re better off using a different model if you’re at that stage. reply hungryhobbit 6 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] It has absolutely nothing to do with the model. Use Fable if you want. Hell, get some secret new model: I still guarantee (for any serious project, meaty enough to demonstrate this ... like the OP's defense): the model will hallucinate some stuff and omit some stuff. It's just what all models do. This adversarial approach is a well-known way to work around the issues all LLMs have (or at least, all so far). reply garciasn 6 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] The point is that Anthropic will be using Claude (although likely an internal / unreleased version) and to get it to the point where Claude is reporting it's clear in the hopes that Anthropic's internal version will as well. While I agree you should be using multiple models for something like this, that misses the point the parent was making. reply enlyth 9 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Hah, I do this all the time with my code. Normally you write something with the help of Claude, and then ask for a review. What's the reviewer gonna do? Ask Claude to review it. So I just skip straight to doing that myself with a second Claude session reply anigbrowl 8 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] Nothing personal, but I think this is terrible advice. Somehow we've normalized technology companies making arbitrary judgments and acting as their own appeals process, while putting the onus on users to prove their innocence of substance- and detail-free accusations. Accepting these Kafkaesque asymmetries as normal is not the mark of a healthy society. reply DonsDiscountGas 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Because OP isn't in danger of going to prison. Companies get to refuse service to potential customers if they want to. reply bigfatkitten 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] They could’ve just nuked OP’s account on the spot if they wanted to. Dealing with vendors has risks. If you rely on a vendor to make money, then you need to have a plan for if that vendor stops being available (their service goes down, they go broke, or they ban you.) reply anon373839 46 minutes ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] > Companies get to refuse service to potential customers if they want to. But Anthropic has stated that it should/will be the only AI provider that lasts, the "winner" that "takes all" (in Anthropic's own words). It has also stated that its product will subsume all human economic activity. These are preposterous ideas. But if that is the ambition they are working toward, I don't think they should be allowed to refuse service to whomever they wish. reply ricree 7 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Which is going to be wonderful consolation if any of these companies ever achieves the sort of monopolistic hold over the economy that their valuations suggest they are aiming for. reply brudgers 3 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] It’s just: No shirt. No shoes. No service. If you want rights, negotiate a contract and lawyer up. reply techjamie 6 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] The is why, when my various cybersecurity projects get flagged and refused, I justify why I'm asking it to perform the action and usually get it to agree with me that it's the right course, but the filter won't let it proceed. That way if they ever get on my case, my assumption is if there's a human review at all, it's probably just Claude pointing out pieces and giving an opinion, then a human hits the button. Or, more likely, there is no human reviewing it and it's Claude all the way down. Either way, by getting Claude to agree with me in the moment, I'm hopefully keeping myself out of the crosshairs. reply operatingthetan 9 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] >submit the same evidence to Claude and ask it to tell you if it's sufficient evidence to make distilling seem unlikely. Or they will read their logs and determine this is evidence of them trying to distill. reply baxtr 9 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] This is very good advice since they will anyway use a Claude agent to review your submission. reply amelius 8 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] > Because you know Anthropic is just going to be using Claude as well. Yes, but a non-public version that is lightyears ahead. reply OsrsNeedsf2P 9 hours ago | prev | next [–] Migrate to Bedrock via AWS if you're on Anthropic API. If you have any serious bill, you'll get a dedicated account rep who will be an actual human being you can go through to resolve future issues. reply sheepscreek 8 hours ago | parent | next [–] This is a good suggestion. A thought just occurred to me: I believe Bedrock supports ZDR, in that case, how the heck would Anthropic ever know how are the models being used? reply frenchtoast8 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] If you are using any of these models, Bedrock is not ZDR. https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15425695-covered-mode... reply monsieurbanana 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] ZDR doesn't necessarily help with this. If they can determine (or even if they can't, but believe they can) that you're doing distillation from a single of your prompts, they will still flag your account. ZDR doesn't prevent them processing your data. reply _ink_ 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] That's an interesting question. My feeling is, that they also don't want the Bedrock models distilled, so maybe ZDR means something else to them then to us? reply frenchtoast8 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Even when Bedrock is ZDR, AWS is still doing certain automated checks on the input/output. They look for CSAM and also terms of service violations (whatever that means). reply SaucyWrong 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I wouldn’t be surprised if Anthropic is able to build a cumulative risk score that predicts whether a customer is attempting to distill without retaining any data in a way that falls afoul of the ZDR. Also, IIRC from reading the ZDR when I was looking into it, there is a carve-out that permits them to retain data that fails a risk score for breaking laws or attempting to violate safety, and as we know, Anthropic loves to frame distillation as a safety concern. reply leafingensemble 6 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] The answer to this puzzle is that Anthropic on Bedrock has zero data retention, but it retains data. Cue the cartoon villain. reply 0xbadcafebee 8 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] AWS will still disable your Bedrock access to Anthropic if you sneeze too loud. I'm right now writing up an email to AWS to get our production account un-blocked. Sure, a human will review it, but we've still had no access for days. My advice is move to a less-crappy AI provider. I can't convince my teams, but maybe you can yours. reply philipbjorge 5 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] In our case, AWS said Anthropic shut it down and we could only resolve it direct via their TypeForm. reply whywhywhywhy 9 hours ago | prev | next [–] What's the point continuing giving money to a company that treats you like this? They're not the only provider in town. reply fourside 9 hours ago | parent | next [–] Agreed but even if they move to another provider, it’s not something that can be done overnight. reply aleqs 7 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] It can be actually reply throw_m239339 7 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] > Agreed but even if they move to another provider, it’s not something that can be done overnight. what choice does he have? He has 24 hours until Anthropic shuts down their API access. He should get started right now. reply 361994752 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] why? shouldn't it suppose to be as easy as changing an api key? reply kadoban 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] It's not _quite_ that easy. If nothing else you have to find all the things you tested with one model/agent and make sure they still work, make sure the specific wording or tools/skills/whatever exist. reply m00x 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Investing in evals should be something companies do early. I set it up for our company and we're saving 50%+ by being able to route tasks properly and we're not stuck on any provider. reply andai 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Nice. Sounds like you should be selling that. reply plagiarist 7 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Do you have a good framework you like for running evals? reply actusual 7 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] We use Arize internally. reply demo4567 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] invest in evals and switch providers via routers. that is your insurance policy. reply largbae 1 hour ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] This poster clearly _has_ benchmarks and tests, hence the ban. reply baobabKoodaa 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] if you're actually doing something where quality matters, you need to re-tweak your settings and your prompts for whichever model you are switching to. it takes work. reply 627467 6 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Is this really a argument against being prepared for model/provider switching? Hasn't it been demonstrated that even when you pin a model from BigFrontierLab their performance can vary at the whim of their resource allocation decision? reply j45 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Models do not all work the same, or in the same order for all tasks. reply x-complexity 5 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] > They're not the only provider in town. They're the only provider of Opus 5.5, the one specific model that everyone agrees is the current "good enough". The only other model I'm seeing that hits that mark is Gemini 4 Neon. reply largbae 8 hours ago | prev | next [–] If they drop whole accounts for bad prompts, this will become a new attack vector a la SimonW's "lethal trifecta". Make obvious distillation instructions on a website and get social media bots or other prompt injection targets to look it up through their models... reply alexsmirnov 1 hour ago | parent | next [–] I did get Opus requests blocking while agent did web research using search / fetch tools. Something on downloaded page triggered it. So the attack vector is very possible. reply deflator 6 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] A scary possibility. TOS violation injection? reply arjie 9 hours ago | prev | next [–] That's got to suck. You're sure you haven't lost your API keys in some way, right? I've never had to deal with this but that would be my first thought. That someone stole my keys from somewhere and they're actually running distillation. reply prometheus1992 9 hours ago | parent | next [–] they would have gotten a surprise bill if that happened, right? reply arjie 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Indeed, but if they're running a lot of usage, the distillation attack might be hidden in it. They're pretty sophisticated and you can query usage to throttle. A distiller is usually distributing across a large number of keys and they'll do this to keep from being discovered. reply throwup238 9 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] That assumes they’re auditing the bills against internal metrics, which I doubt even most big corps do, let alone startups. reply RGS1811 9 hours ago | prev | next [–] I was doing some totally innocuous work on IRS forms last night and had a subagent flagged for "reasoning extraction". I wonder if they've increased the sensitivity of whatever auto-detection they're doing recently. reply chatmasta 8 hours ago | parent | next [–] It’s happened to me when asking it to look at past session transcripts, export earlier chats as HTML pages, look at tool calls from previous sessions… that sort of thing seems to trigger an overeager classifier. reply demo4567 8 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] invest in evals and switch providers via routers. that is your insurance policy. reply mmaunder 9 hours ago | prev | next [–] This is why we need competition. Being locked out for an individual or company by a single leading AI provider is a death sentence. reply bastawhiz 8 hours ago | parent | next [–] It's not? Get Claude through Bedrock or vertex or foundry if you really need Claude. Or don't build against a single proprietary model. Everyone and their brother has a hot new model these days. AI is arguably the most competitive tech industry right now. Use GPT, grok, Gemini, glm, kimi, mistral, or whatever else solves your problem. There's plenty of open weight models that work just as good for most jobs as frontier models with a bit of elbow grease. reply gorgolo 7 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] > Or don't build against a single proprietary model. Everyone and their brother has a hot new model these days. That's why he said "this is why you need competition". And keep in mind that some of these companies want to make it so there's no competition. It's not something to take for granted. reply cowlevel 1 hour ago | parent | prev | next [–] You don't have to use AI. reply amelius 8 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] Sounds more like we need regulation. And if you don't like the idea of government regulation, you haven't seen a company regulate. reply dawnerd 7 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Bingo. If they want to be a utility then they need regulations like a utility would have. reply protocolture 4 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] >And if you don't like the idea of government regulation, you haven't seen a company regulate. I have seen good and horrendous examples of both tbh. And I mean, a company is a legal fiction created to limit the liability of certain people engaged in a particular enterprise. Anything a company regulates is really just government regulation at the end of the day. reply demo4567 8 hours ago | prev | next [–] Anthropic is not the only game in town. Get an LLM router, switch providers and write your own evals. Who cares what Anthropic's made up garbage ToS are. Stop using them if they don't give you what you need. reply jimnotgym 9 hours ago | prev | next [–] Since proving a negative is hard, my only suggestion is to tell them what it is you have been doing. Ask them what part of that is an issue for them? reply kmeisthax 9 hours ago | parent | next [–] Big Tech categorically refuses to do this. The risk department is full of Maoists. They are judge, jury, and executioner; and if they told you what crime you were guilty of you'd just find an easier way to not get caught. Enumeration is a hard problem so they'd much rather have you look through their policies and overcomply, rather than them spending time and money figuring out what you did wrong so you can undercomply. reply BigTTYGothGF 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] > The risk department is full of Maoists If only. reply lenerdenator 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Eh, Dengists. Willing to accept capitalist reforms but then they institute a policy of using brutal methods to make sure that you meet the production targets needed to put them at the top of the market. reply thomasjeff1 8 hours ago | prev | next [–] How is distilling different from scraping the internet, books, journals, literature etc? reply bryan_w 7 hours ago | parent | next [–] It's not, but just like the internet, If you want to stop people from scraping you, you can. This is pretty straightforward reply cowlevel 1 hour ago | parent | prev | next [–] It's not, and it's equally adversarial. Both sides are working as hard as possible to make sure their side wins. Anthropic just happens to be on a different side of each. reply plagiarist 7 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] It is harming billionaires instead of plebs. reply prometheus1992 9 hours ago | prev | next [–] Ditch anthropic. reply anigbrowl 8 hours ago | prev | next [–] you don't. Hire a lawyer to draft a letter saying in substance 'false accusations, deliberate or negligent, are an attack on our business and we will not be bullied.' reply sebzim4500 8 hours ago | parent | next [–] They aren't making public accusations so there is no slander/libel argument. The only potential case you could possibly make is to claim they have violated their contract, but unless they had Haiku draft their TOS that sounds unlikely to work. Ultimately they can refuse service to whoever they want. reply 15155 3 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] What are your damages? How would any third party learn of Anthropics desire to discontinue business with you unless you make it known? reply 0xbadcafebee 8 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] Dario will be shaking in his trillion dollar boots reply dabinat 7 hours ago | prev | next [–] I personally believe that building a business entirely dependent on someone else’s product that they control is very dangerous. I would recommend figuring out a way to generalize so you can swap providers as needed and not have it be a big deal. It’ll take some time and resources up front but it’ll be worth it in the flexibility you’ll have that will allow your company to stay nimble. reply robmsmt 8 hours ago | prev | next [–] Part of the reason we started building our company. We got a similar message and realized we could not depend on one provider. It’s a huge risk reply BikiniPrince 9 hours ago | prev | next [–] Distillation attacks are spread throughout numerous accounts. You have likely triggered some detection. I think the best approach would be to show your work is part of a real project. As long as you can defend your API usage it should be possible to demonstrate your work has been legitimate. If you have outliers, like you mentioned then explain them. reply iamdamian 8 hours ago | parent | next [–] Can we avoid playing into the Anthropic narrative that distillation is an “attack”? reply hashmap 7 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] maybe. claude itself is the product of a distillation attack. reply BikiniPrince 6 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Playing word games won’t help him. Anthropic clearly believes he is part of a large scale attack on their service. reply Blackthorn 7 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] Calling them "attacks" is begging the question. reply platevoltage 7 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] Now you get to prove to the AI companies that you're using their product that you pay for "correctly". Great industry we have here. reply demo4567 8 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] that is not an "attack" except on "anthropic's cash inflow" which is competition. reply cowlevel 1 hour ago | root | parent | next [–] Yes, companies attack each other as part of competition, and they also defend themselves. That's the reality of competition. reply jtrn 8 hours ago | prev | next [–] How do you know that someone doesn't has a infected computer or an api key owned by your company has not leaked and is used for distilling? reply kbelder 7 hours ago | parent | next [–] Should they also be required to prove that nobody has stolen any of their keys? And that there is no malware on any of their computers? reply varispeed 9 hours ago | prev | next [–] This is why I don't use Anthropic for any serious work, when it has flagged normal work for cyber security exploit many times and stopping the session, forcing me to start over and lose money. reply demo4567 8 hours ago | prev | next [–] invest in evals and switch providers via routers. that is your insurance policy. reply itintheory 8 hours ago | parent | next [–] You've posted this a lot in this thread. What does it mean? reply georgemcbay 9 hours ago | prev | next [–] I have no help to give to OP as I can't imagine how you can prove a negative in this situation, and I have no idea if the OP is innocent or not... but this situation highlights how crazy things would be if the AI-provider landscape really did settle into a monopoly or duopoly. Every single person or organization would be one or two misunderstandings from being irrevocably economically handicapped. reply recursive 9 hours ago | parent | next [–] I think it's worse than that. Most people will just get unconditionally economically handicapped as an "unfortunate side effect of progress". Knowledge work won't have much value in a post-knowledge society. Controlling the weights and the means of inference will accumulate most of that value. reply georgemcbay 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] > I think it's worse than that. Most people will just get unconditionally economically handicapped as an "unfortunate side effect of progress". Knowledge work won't have much value in a post-knowledge society. Yeah, I was more thinking in the shorter term where AI still needs human babysitters for most knowledge work. On a longer timeline (and 'longer' is doing some heavy lifting here, since I don't think it will take that long) we're all just kind of fucked without massive upheavals in how our socioeconomic systems work (which I don't have a lot of faith in going smoothly given where we are now economically and politically). I suppose my fallback when we reach that point is a life of crime. > Controlling the weights and the means of inference will accumulate most of that value. 個人の実験的なプロジェクトです。 日常の作業環境として使えるほど完成してはいません。 動作を確かめているのは、 新しくインストールした Debian 13 に導入スクリプトで入れた場合だけです。 すでに使っている環境（ほかのデスクトップ環境やディスプレイマネージャが入っているものなど）への導入は試していません。 試すときは、仮想マシンや試験用のマシンをおすすめします。 これは何？ Windows XP の explorer.exe を、パッチを当てた Wine の上で Linux のデスクトップシェル として動かすプロジェクトです。 タスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、フォルダウィンドウは XP 本物のものです。Linux のアプリも、XP の枠とタスクバーで扱えます。 Microsoft のファイルは同梱していません。お手元の XP の ISO から、必要なファイルだけを取り出して使います。 XP の ISO が無い方は、XP のシェルの代わりに ReactOS のシェル （Windows 2000 風のクラシックの見た目）でも 試せます。ReactOS は自由なソフトウェアなので、導入スクリプトが公式のリリースから取得します（ docs/reactos.md ）。 Windows 7 の ISO があれば、 Windows 7 のシェル （Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目）でも試せます。まだ実験的な試作です（ docs/windows7.md ）。 できること XP のシェル : Luna（またはクラシック）のタスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、マイ コンピュータ、フォルダウィンドウ。 Linux アプリとの統合 : Linux のウィンドウに XP の枠が付き、タスクバー、Alt+Tab、最小化・最大化が XP と同じように動きます。 Linux のアプリは「すべてのプログラム」に並びます。 通知領域 : Linux のトレイアイコン（StatusNotifierItem と XEmbed）が XP の通知領域に出ます。 XP 自身のネットワーク・バッテリー・音量のアイコンと、そのフライアウト（音量、電源メーター、ワイヤレス ネットワーク接続の状態）も 出ます。NetworkManager と PipeWire / PulseAudio の状態から作ります（ AshesTom さんのフォーク の XP Explorer から）。 ワイヤレス ネットワークの一覧から、初めてのネットワークにも XP のネットワーク キーの画面で接続できます。メニューや画面の文字は ISO の XP のファイルから読みます。 XP Explorer からの追加 : フォルダの左のタスク ペイン、画面のプロパティ（Windows XP とクラシックのテーマ、スタイルと配色。 配色は ISO の HIVEDEF.INF と themeui.dll から作ります）、画像の縮小版とプレビュー、XP のサウンド（起動、ログオン、ログオフも）、 ネットワーク接続、Internet Explorer 6、Windows Media Player 9、スタートメニューの左の列（インターネット、電子メール、 よく使うプログラム）。どれもお手元の ISO のファイルで動きます（ prefix/extras.py ）。 キーボードの配列 : 最初は Linux のシステムの配列（ localectl ）です。コントロール パネルの「地域と言語のオプション」→ 「言語」→「詳細」（XP 自身のもの）で入力言語を足したり既定を変えたりすると、セッションの配列（Wayland では labwc、 X11 では setxkbmap）がすぐに従います。2 つ以上なら XP と同じ左 Alt+Shift で切り替わります（ session/keyboard.py ）。 日本語入力 : fcitx5 + Mozc です。Ctrl+Space（または全角/半角）で切り替えます。GTK、Qt、Wine のアプリで使えます。 日本語版と英語版の XP : どちらの ISO でも動きます。言語は ISO から自動で判断し、字体（英語版は Tahoma など）、 ロケール、ようこそ画面をその XP に合わせます（英語版では日本語入力は設定しません）。 Windows のアプリ : WoW64 の Wine 11.0 で、32bit と 64bit のアプリが動きます。端末で wine setup.exe と打つと、 インストーラーが作るショートカットは XP のスタートメニューに入ります。 XP のようこそ画面 : LightDM の greeter として、XP のようこそ画面とログオフの画面を出せます（任意）。 シェルが起動するまでは XP と同じ大きな「ようこそ」の画面を出します。 XP のキー操作 : Windows キー、Ctrl+Esc、Win+R、Win+E が使えます。 クイック起動 : タスクバーの右クリック →「ツール バー」→「クイック起動」で出せます（XP と ReactOS。Windows 7 は実機と同じく 「新規ツール バー」でクイック起動のフォルダを選びます）。スタートメニューから Linux のアプリのショートカットも置けます。 「デスクトップの表示」も実機と同じく、もう一度押すと窓が元に戻ります。 画面の拡大（DPI） : XP と同じ「DPI 設定」で、文字や部品を大きくできます（96・120・144 など）。 落ちても戻れる : XP のシェルが繰り返し落ちると、Wine 標準の explorer と xterm に切り替わります。 Wayland のセッション（任意・X11 のセッション以上に実験的） : X11 のウィンドウマネージャーの代わりに、パッチを当てた labwc で 動かすセッションです（XP、ReactOS、Windows 7 のシェル）。モニターごとの倍率や 125%・150% などの倍率が使え、シェルはぼけずに描かれます。 Wayland のアプリにもシェルの枠が付きます。作ったばかりで、確かめた範囲は X11 のセッションより狭く、既知の制限もあります（ docs/wayland.md ）。 ふだん試すなら X11 のセッションをおすすめします。 ReactOS のシェル（任意） : XP の ISO の代わりに ReactOS 0.4.16 の explorer で動かすセッションです。日本語と英語に対応します。 XP のシェルと並べて入れられます。 Windows 7 のシェル（任意・実験的） : Windows 7 SP1 x64 の explorer で動かすセッションです（Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目。 Aero のガラスはまだありません）。スタートメニュー、タスクバー、通知領域、フォルダの窓が動き、Linux のアプリもアプリごとに タスクバーにまとまります。確かめたのは日本語版と、その文字を英語の言語パックのものに入れ替えた英語版です。 XP のクラシック（ --theme classic ） ReactOS のシェル（ --shell reactos 。XP の ISO は要りません） Windows 7 のシェル（ --shell win7 。実験的） タスクバーの「小さいアイコンを使う」と「結合しない」（すぐに切り替わります） Windows 7 のログオン画面（ --greeter ） 試してみる Windows XP Professional SP3（x86）の ISO（日本語版か英語版）を ご自身で 用意してください。 新しくインストールした Debian 13 に、ログインして使う利用者として入り、次を実行します。 git clone https://github.com/mikuta0407/win4wine.git ~ /win4wine cd ~ /win4wine scripts/setup.sh --media /path/to/WindowsXPSP3.iso --greeter 再起動すると、XP のようこそ画面からそのまま XP のシェルに入ります。 XP の ISO が無いときは、ReactOS のシェルで試せます（ISO は要りません）。 scripts/setup.sh --shell reactos --lang ja # 英語なら --lang en ログイン画面でセッション「ReactOS Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。 Windows 7 のシェル（実験的）は、Windows 7 SP1 x64 の ISO から作ります。 scripts/setup.sh --shell win7 --media /path/to/Windows7SP1x64.iso ログイン画面でセッション「Windows 7 Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。 詳しい手順とオプションは 🔗 導入手順（INSTALL.md） にあります。Wine をソースからビルドするので、4 コアで 1 時間半ほどかかります。 テーマ（XP のクラシックなど）と文字の大きさは、後から変えられます（ 見た目と文字の大きさを変える ）。 注意 Warning Windows XP（と Windows 7）の ISO はご自身で入手してください。 このリポジトリにも導入スクリプトにも、Microsoft のファイルを 取得する処理はありません。ISO と取り出したファイルの扱いは、Microsoft の使用許諾に従ってください。 利用は自己責任でお願いします。 データの損失や不具合について、作者は責任を負いません。 Microsoft とも Wine プロジェクトとも関係のない、非公式のプロジェクトです。 確かめているのは日本語版と英語版の XP SP3（x86）だけです。ほかの言語の XP も英語版と同じ設定で入れるので動くかもしれませんが、 一切試していません（ setup.sh は警告を出して続けます）。 仕組み LightDM ─ XP のようこそ画面 (greeter/) └─ XP Shell セッション (session/supervisor.py) ├─ Wine 11.0 + 151 本のパッチ (wine/patches/) │ └─ XP の explorer.exe, shell32.dll, …（ISO から取り出したもの。ReactOS や Windows 7 のシェルではそれらのもの） ├─ bridge-wm: X11 のウィンドウマネージャー + Win32 の代理ウィンドウ (bridge-wm/) │ （Wayland のセッションでは、ウィンドウマネージャーの代わりにパッチを当てた labwc。wayland/） └─ fcitx5 + Mozc, トレイの仲介 (bridge-wm/tray.py) 仕組みや設計の詳しい説明は docs/ にまとめています。 似たプロジェクト loss32 : Wine の上の Win32 のソフトウェアだけでデスクトップを作る Linux ディストリビューションの計画です。 ReactOS の部品も使います。win4wine が XP 本物のシェルを Debian の上で動かすのに対し、loss32 は自由なソフトウェアだけで作ります。 守っていること Windows 由来のバイナリには手を加えません。違いは Wine とその周辺で吸収します。 Microsoft のバイナリを逆アセンブルしません。挙動は公開 API と、実際の XP の上で動かす自作のプローブで調べています。 Microsoft のファイル、取り出したもの、Wine の prefix は、Git 管理外の localres/ と .local/ にだけ置きます。 貢献してくださった方 AshesTom さん（ フォーク ）: XP の画面のプロパティ、 サウンド、キーボードの配列、通知領域の XP のアイコン、スタートメニューの左の列、Internet Explorer 6 と Windows Media Player 9、 起動中のようこそ画面、タイトルバーのアニメーションと小さいアイコン、Arch Linux への対応、 xp.sh など。 ライセンス LGPL-2.1-or-later （Wine と同じ）です。対象はこのリポジトリのコードとパッチだけです。 ただし wayland/patches/labwc/ は labwc と同じ GPL-2.0-only、 wayland/patches/wlroots/ は wlroots と同じ MIT です。 Windows XP と Windows 7 のファイルと、スクリーンショットに写っている XP と Windows 7 の画面の著作権は Microsoft にあります。 ReactOS のシェルで使う ReactOS のファイルは、ReactOS のライセンス（GPL-2.0-or-later、DLL の多くは LGPL-2.1-or-later）に従います。 About Windows XP の Explorer を Wine 上で title: Kagi Mail (public beta)
body_text: Kagi Blog - Kagi Mail is here (Public Beta) Skip to content Menu Close Products Assistant Mail News Translate Maps Summarize API Overview Docs Pricing Pricing Overview API Kagi for Teams Libraries Blog Sign up for free Sign in All Posts Copy link Kagi Mail is here (Public Beta) # Announcements November 23, 2026 5 min read We are proud to announce something that our small team of very dedicated people at Kagi has been building for a long time â the public beta of Kagi Mail . A private email and calendar with a @kagimail.com address, or with your own domains. If youâve already swapped Google Search for Kagi and Chrome for Orion, your inbox is probably the last big piece of your digital life still at Google. Now you can move that too. Try Kagi Mail free for 60 days $99/year (+ Sales Tax) after that. Included with Kagi Ultimate. Why we built it Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once. There are great ones out there, and weâre fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way . For email, that job is to be fast, private, and secure. On top of that, it should help you stay on track with whatâs important: bring forward what you need to act on, respond to, or acknowledge, and quietly handle the rest. Kagi Mail also has to treat you the way Kagi Search and Orion do: no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in. Already a Kagi member? Kagi Mail is included in Ultimate . Sign in with your Kagi account, and youâre set. AI features draw from your existing Allowance. On another plan, or no Kagi account yet? After the free 60-day trial, you can get Kagi Mail for $99/year (+ Sales Tax). How it works: A service and a client, on open standards To deliver the experience we believe in, we built the full stack: hosting for your addresses and domains, plus the mail and calendar apps. It runs on open standards and open-source infrastructure (the Stalwart server, IMAP, JMAP, and CalDAV), so you can use Kagiâs apps or any compatible client you already like. The basics A @kagimail.com address Unlimited aliases Unlimited domains Built-in Calendar 50 GB of storage Intelligence Organize your mail in your own words. Brief it the way youâd brief an assistant: âLabel anything where beta users send product feedback. It might come from @kagimail.com, but use judgment.â You decide what permissions each rule gets (read the content, or skip the inbox). Inbox Highlights show what needs you today, and learn from what you dismiss. Ask your inbox in plain language and get direct answers with the source email, including text inside scanned PDFs and photos. Newsletter view reads newsletters like a feed, out of the way of real mail. Responsible AI, with one switch to turn it all off. You control what AI is allowed to do and infer . Private by default Tracking pixels and remote images are blocked or proxied, so senders canât tell when or where you opened their mail. Sender screening holds new senders until you approve them, so they never reach your inbox uninvited. Suspicious senders trigger a phishing warning, while verified senders show their (BMI) logo. No ads, ever. No profiling, no selling, no sharing your data. For teams and families Shared addresses on your domain (team@, info@, family@): create an alias, then choose which people have access to it Sign in through a social login, or your organizationâs own identity provider (OIDC) Coming soon: Shared mailboxes Kagi integration Kagi Translate is built in Email Assistant: Write to assistant@kagimail.com for answers about your mail (actions coming soon) Proofread and translation included while you write emails For power users and developers Keyboard-first: command palette, shortcuts, and search operators Rule-based filtering with Sieve, no AI involved MCP server with read access to your mail Works with Apple Mail, Thunderbird, and any IMAP/JMAP/CalDAV client, with automatic setup Whatâs not here yet We will keep adding new capabilities â hereâs what to expect over the next few quarters. Feature Target Contacts and address book Q1 2027 Full Kagi Assistant integration Q1 2027 Native mobile apps Q3 2027 Until the mobile apps arrive, use the mobile web app or any IMAP/JMAP client, such as Apple Mail or Thunderbird. Our âno lock-inâ promise to you Leaving Kagi Mail is as easy as joining it. Your mail, calendar, and workflows are yours, and you can export them at any time, through standard protocols and a one-click export experience. Youâll keep access to your mailbox for six months after leaving Kagi Mail. You can send and receive emails for the first 60 days, then read and export your mail with one click for the remaining four months. We build an ecosystem so things work better together for those who want it, not to trap anyone . Try Kagi Mail free for 60 days $99/year (+ Sales Tax) after that. Included with Kagi Ultimate. We want Kagi Mail to be the first email account weâd create for our children. Weâre not there yet, but it is a high bar we hold ourselves to, and every feature in this beta is a step toward it: a calm, safe place to communicate, and a window onto an internet that treats you as a person, not a product whoâs been tracked, targeted, and sold to. We can build it this way because of you. Kagi has no ad business, and no one pushing us to monetize your inbox; youâre not a dataset for ads or AI. You are here because you believe the internet can be built differently. Thank you. title: Yes, 17M lines of Lean is a lot
body_text: Yes, 17m lines of Lean is a lot | micjm micjm blog about subscribe Yes, 17m lines of Lean is a lot 2026-11-22 AI disclosure: I wrote all text here, but used Agent Duel (an open source battle system on top of OpenCode) to research sources of Lean proofs and generate charts. The recent proof of the Riemann hypothesis came with a statistic attached: the proof is 17 million lines of Lean. Beyond the philosophical questions of what it means to have a proof longer than any human could comprehend, I’m left with a simpler question: is that as large as it sounds? To investigate, I hunted for collections of Lean proofs online. I found two and charted the lengths of their proofs. (All charts have a log x axis, which makes 17m lines look a lot closer to 1m and 100k than it really is.) Famous theorems in Mathlib Mathlib maintains a collection of famous proofs. There are over 1k but only 259 have Lean associated, which I chart here. These are all human generated, and as we can see, they come nowhere close to 17m. Every Lean package on Reservoir Reservoir indexes every published Lean package, 938 of which have Lean code on GitHub. This one has a lot more data, including AI assisted proofs. We even have a few that are over 16m!: 88m: Qiuzhen-CFSG/CFSG this appears to be an AI built proof that is still a work in progress. 36m: CBirkbeck/LeanBridge , a project linking the LMFDB database of number theory objects to Mathlib. This isn’t really a proof: about 98% of its Lean is files generated by scripts that check the database’s numbers one by one. The hand-written part is closer to 500k lines. 27m: anthropics/fermats-last-theorem is another Anthropic special: a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, published on GitHub in September. Its README says “the Lean sources were produced by AI agents building on human-written open-source Lean”, including the human FLT project led by Kevin Buzzard, which is about 60k lines and still in progress. The AI version is roughly 450 times longer. So yes, 17m lines is a lot. What I'm working on Agent Duel - a battle system on top of OpenCode

title: The next circle of security hell
body_text: The next circle of security hell – Michał Górny Skip to content Michał Górny Retroactively fixing the world Menu Homepage The next circle of security hell A few years back I wrote “The modern packager’s security nightmare” . Have things improved since? On the contrary, I feel like we’re slipping down a well-oiled slope with no end in sight. Vulnerabilities are reported at unprecedented rates. A lot of people are doing everything they can to patch them up, which doesn’t necessarily mean they’re not making things even worse. Complex software involves complex trees of dependencies, and every branch on that tree needs tending to. When they stop being reliable, people further down the tree start taking more weight. And there’s a limit of how much a single person can do, so what started as an effort to resolve an issue upstream may quickly become a weakness. Is software less secure these days? It’s tempting to say yes. I’d love to blame the corporate sector for egotistically dumping low quality software on us. I’d love to blame marketing-oriented people developing stuff with the sole goal of making a profit. I’d love to blame Rust for getting people obsessed about memory safety, and ignoring the kinds of vulnerabilities that aren’t caught by the compiler. Finally, I’d really love to blame slop. But the truth is, I don’t know. That’s really beside the point. The point is that nowadays everyone and their chatbot became security researchers. Projects are being flooded with vulnerability reports. Even though pretty much every bug bounty was discontinued because of slop, people aren’t stopping. And even if we disregard truly invalid junk reports, there’s a lot left, and you have to deal with them somehow. You have to figure out how important they are, and how to fix them (or more likely, whether the fixes submitted are truly valid and don’t introduce regressions), or if you should reject them and why. In the end, security is tricky. We’re seeing lots of bugs like REDoS, or other kinds of “performance bugs”. Are they really vulnerabilities? Well, it depends on the attack vector. And that in turn depends on how the software is used. Some scenarios are really contrived, and feel like “shell can execute dangerous commands if you type them in”. But then, you also have really serious issues such as “timing attack can be used to guess user’s secret”. You need to know a lot to make that kind of judgment, and sometimes your judgment doesn’t really match users’ expectations. In the end, what can project maintainers do? Even if they have the expertise and the energy to judge, if they can “know better”, there’s likely a CVE assigned already. It may have absurdly high score. All security scanners will complain unless you fix it, and users will come asking or complaining, or attacking, or forking. I mean, technology can’t handle nuances. More than once I’ve been doing unnecessary security stabilizations over vulnerabilities that didn’t affect Gentoo (for example, because we already unbundled the vulnerable dependencies), to avoid false positives from security scanners. I’ve been also doing meaningless version bumps (with no real changes or no changes that applied to Gentoo) so that our packages don’t get reported as being “outdated”. It’s a hassle and it sucks, but it saves people from worrying. I’ve said this before and I’ll say it again: most projects aren’t really prepared to handle security issues. And it’s not just about triage. It’s about having LTS or security branches, it’s about making proper security releases with minimal changes. Unfortunately, it’s quite common for security fixes to be combined with new features, deprecations, API changes. In extreme cases, people are caught with their metaphorical pants down, and suddenly need to make a security release in the middle of a major rewrite, or along with barely tested new code. And then, people downstream discover that they need to quickly deal with major API changes to upgrade past a vulnerable version. These things keep piling up. What happens next? The community reaches a breaking point. People can’t keep up. You discover you can’t rely on others, so you work around them. You start bundling more stuff. Soon enough your workload goes beyond your ability. Software development becomes “every chatbot for itself”. The nightmare becomes worse, and the wheel keeps turning. Author Michał Górny Posted on 2026-10-27 2026-10-28 Categories Security 2 thoughts on “The next circle of security hell” Jukka says: 2026-10-31 at 16:15 Thanks for the good work. And a small note regarding: “Unfortunately, it’s quite common for security fixes to be combined with new features, deprecations, API changes.” The CRA tried to address this issue, but unfortunately left the door open for this kind of bundling. While I prefer LTS-style releases (and I do not currently have fast enough machines to run Gentoo comfortably), I’d suppose the bundling is even more common in the closed source world. But regarding the gloomy conclusion: maybe there is also something positive; maybe the days of zero days will also be eventually over? Reply Pelito says: 2026-11-18 at 21:40 > But regarding the gloomy conclusion: maybe there is also something positive; maybe the days of zero days will also be eventually over? They won’t. Neither humans nor machines are infallible, so bugs will always slip. Detection by a non-deterministic machine on snapshots of the world is also bound to leave the maintainers blind to some issue that a third party actually saw. So, no, while zero days will probably normalize in volume after we pick up the slack, there will always be new ones and there will always be a few ones we miss long enough for them to be exploited. Photograph: Esa/PA View image in fullscreen Artist's impression of the two BepiColombo orbiters, which will use a host of instruments to unravel Mercury's mysteries. Photograph: Esa/PA Space Spacecraft reaches Mercury on second-ever mission to enter its orbit BepiColombo double probe will map planet’s surface and study its interior to shed light on its unusually large core Ian Sample Science editor Thu 19 Nov 2026 19.01 EST Last modified on Tue 24 Nov 2026 11.37 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google After a voyage of more than eight years and 6bn miles, a joint European-Japanese space mission has arrived at Mercury and is preparing to swing into orbit around the tiny, barely explored world. The BepiColombo mission will become only the second in history to circle the first rock from the sun and the smallest planet in the solar system when flight controllers fire the spacecraft’s thrusters on Saturday and send it into orbit. For researchers, the €1.6bn (£1.4bn) mission is the best hope yet of understanding how Mercury formed so close to the sun, why it has a magnetic field, and what makes up the frozen ice that lurks in the planet’s permanently shadowed craters. “We’re very excited, it’s been a long wait,” said Prof Emma Bunce at the University of Leicester, who has worked on the project for 20 years. Getting to Mercury poses unusual difficulties. Because the planet is near the centre of the solar system, spacecraft accelerate under the sun’s gravity and must spend much of their time braking to avoid shooting straight past. “It’s a very complex and challenging mission,” said Bunce, the principal investigator on an instrument called the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer, or MIXS, which will analyse the geochemical composition of the planet’s surface. View image in fullscreen A photo made available by the European Space Agency in October 2021 shows a view of Mercury captured by the BepiColombo mission. Photograph: European Space Agency/AFP/Getty Images It will be some months before scientists can start observing Mercury. In early December, the spacecraft will separate into two orbiters, one European, the other Japanese, which will manoeuvre to different polar orbits around the planet. Science operations are due to start in April next year. The European probe, named the Mercury Planetary Orbiter or MPO, will map the planet’s surface and composition at high resolution, and study Mercury’s interior to shed light on its unusually large core. Its Japanese partner will measure the planet’s magnetic field and its sodium exosphere, the extremely thin layer of gas and atoms that surrounds the planet. Mercury is only 50% larger than the moon but has four times its mass. One question the mission will explore is why the rock is so dense. Prof Geraint Jones, the lead project scientist on BepiColombo at the European Space Agency, said anticipation of the scientific results had kept everyone enthused during the spacecraft’s eight-year journey . “We’re expecting to learn a huge amount, bringing more powerful instruments on two spacecraft to study all aspects of the planet – its interior, surface, and the space around it,” he said. Mercury is a planet of extremes. The tiny world takes 58 Earth days to rotate on its axis but just 88 Earth days to orbit the sun. This results in a solar day – or the time it takes for the sun to return to the same position in the sky – lasting 176 Earth days. The sun stays above Mercury’s horizon for half that time, meaning a given patch of ground is in sunlight for about three months. When the sun sets, the same patch will be in darkness for the following three months. In the day, ground temperatures reach 450C while at night they drop to -180C. Jones said: “As well as cameras covering a wide range of wavelengths to study the surface, we’ll be ‘tasting’ the gases around the planet, sensing the magnetic field, probing the interior with ultrasensitive instruments, and mapping the shape of the whole planet with a laser.” The spacecraft are expected to orbit Mercury for about three years, after which they will run out of fuel, lose altitude and ultimately slam into the surface. “Sadly, they are not coming back,” said Bunce. This article was amended on 24 November 2026 to give further detail on why Mercury experiences days and nights that each last about three Earth months. Expert-Tested Gear News + Stories Home News Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to Standardize Parts to Lower Costs Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to Standardize Parts to Lower Costs Japan’s automakers will work together to lower production costs as they band together to compete against China’s growing automotive sector. By Jack Fitzgerald Published: Nov 20, 2026 Save Tomohiro Ohsumi | Getty Images Toyota , Nissan , and Honda will begin standardizing some vehicle parts in an effort to lower production costs, according to a report by Automotive News . The automakers will start with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. Discussions are starting with Japan’s domestic suppliers, though international suppliers will be looped in soon. Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News . The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week. In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact. For Sale Near You See all results for used Toyota for sale near 90017 CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images | Getty Images The first discussions of standardization are set to include Japan’s domestic automotive parts suppliers, though international suppliers will be brought into the fold in time. The first standardization efforts are set to go into place next year, according to the AN report. The push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan’s seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. The automakers are said to hope that they can channel the money saved by homogenizing into new innovations. “We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change,” Sato said. “Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas.” Related News Honda Reveals New Details about Next Hybrid System Honda Will Build a New $3 Billion Factory in Ohio Nissan and Honda Team Up on Software, Electronics ➡️ Skip the lot. title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'
body_text: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’ | Pancreas cancer | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Close dialogue 1 / 1 Next image Previous image Toggle caption Print subscriptions Newsletters Sign in US US edition UK edition Australia edition Europe edition International edition The Guardian - Back to home The Guardian News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Show more Hide expanded menu News View all News US news US politics Midterms 2026 World news Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness Opinion View all Opinion The Guardian view Columnists Letters Opinion videos Cartoons Sport View all Sport Soccer NFL Tennis MLB MLS NBA WNBA NHL F1 Golf Culture View all Culture Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world Lifestyle View all Lifestyle The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money Search input google-search Search Support us Print subscriptions Newsletters Download the app Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us The Guardian app Video Podcasts Pictures Inside the Guardian Guardian Weekly Crosswords Puzzles & games Corrections Tips Search input google-search Search Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45 % of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA View image in fullscreen A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45 % of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA Pancreas cancer Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’ Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing Helena Horton Fri 20 Nov 2026 04.36 EST Last modified on Sat 21 Nov 2026 00.07 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades. In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body. Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission. ‘The undruggable became druggable’: a gamechanging treatment for the world’s deadliest cancer – podcast Read more Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK and has a similarly poor prognosis globally. Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans. A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year. Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread. He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said. FDA gives expedited approval to new groundbreaking pancreatic cancer drug Read more “The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.” Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment, which works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations found in most pancreatic cancers. These mutations drive tumour growth. There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers because they can have similar mutations. Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, said more research was needed, but added: “This is the biggest leap forward we’ve seen in decades for pancreatic cancer patients and could offer real hope to people facing one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat cancers. “These results raise the exciting possibility that this breakthrough could eventually pave the way for treating other cancers that carry Kras gene mutations. More trials are now needed before this treatment can be assessed for use on the NHS and despite this advance, pancreatic cancer survival is still very low.” Explore more on these topics Pancreas cancer Cancer research Medical research Drugs Health news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Cancer diagnoses in England hit record high of more than 1,000 people a day 5 Nov 2026 Woman told she had cancer by NHS worker who inappropriately accessed her records 21 Oct 2026 New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie, study suggests 19 Oct 2026 Pope Leo lung cancer surgery: what kind of operation did he have and what happens next? 16 Oct 2026 Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer as growth removed during surgery 13 Oct 2026 double quotation mark The Guardian view on cancers in under-50s: the risks of obesity must be confronted 8 Oct 2026 ‘Cancer is tripling and will keep increasing’: first African to lead global action against disease ready for battle 8 Oct 2026 Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research finds 6 Oct 2026 Cancer jab can eradicate entire tumours in patients, trial shows 30 May 2026 Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Original reporting and incisive analysis, direct from the Guardian every morning Sign up for our email About us Help Complaints & corrections Contact us Tip us off SecureDrop Privacy policy Cookie policy Tax strategy Terms & conditions All topics All writers Newsletters Digital newspaper archive Bluesky Facebook Instagram LinkedIn Threads TikTok YouTube Advertise with us Guardian Labs Work with us Accessibility settings Back to top © 2026 Guardian News & Media Limited or its affiliated companies. body_text: A beginner's guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth | GPU Partner Skip to content GPU partner Inventory ▾ Systems Memory Storage GPU Cloud Compute View all inventory → Resources ▾ Blog Announcements VRAM calculator Reference Workloads Contact About Build a system Reach a human Build a system Reach a human Home / Blog A beginner's guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it. By Jerry James · Nov 22, 2026 With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle. OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience. That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI : a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware. Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too. Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times). The short version Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it. What Do You Need to Run a Local AI at Home? Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list: A Windows PC with a graphics card (GPU). The more video memory (VRAM) it has, the bigger the model it can run. I'm using an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for this setup. Unsloth Desktop. A free app that 'serves' the AI model to you through a chat interface. Get it from Unsloth . An AI model sized to fit your GPU. We'll pick one in the next section. That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required. Which AI Model Can Your GPU Run? It depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations. On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in. What Is Quantization? Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster. The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2. If you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable. Which Model Should You Run for Your VRAM? For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits. Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator . At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare. If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs . If you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start. Size VRAM Models to try Version (quant) Context size Cards at this size Small 8-12 GB Qwen3.5-9B , Gemma 4 12B UD-Q4_K_S or Q4_K_M 8K-16K RTX 5060 8GB , RTX 3060 12GB , RTX 5070 12GB Medium 16 GB Qwen3-14B , gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE) Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M 16K-32K RTX 5060 Ti 16GB , RTX 5070 Ti , RTX 5080 , RTX PRO 2000 Large 24 GB Gemma 4 31B , Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini UD-Q4_K_M or Q4_K_S 16K-32K RTX 3090 , RTX 4090 , RX 7900 XTX , RTX PRO 4000 Extra Large 32 GB+ Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini UD-Q4_K_XL or Q6_K 64K-128K+ RTX 5090 32GB , RTX PRO 4500 32GB , RTX PRO 5000 48GB , RTX PRO 6000 96GB Small VRAM 8-12 GB Models to try Qwen3.5-9B , Gemma 4 12B Version (quant) UD-Q4_K_S or Q4_K_M Context size 8K-16K Cards at this size RTX 5060 8GB , RTX 3060 12GB , RTX 5070 12GB Medium VRAM 16 GB Models to try Qwen3-14B , gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE) Version (quant) Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M Context size 16K-32K Cards at this size RTX 5060 Ti 16GB , RTX 5070 Ti , RTX 5080 , RTX PRO 2000 Large VRAM 24 GB Models to try Gemma 4 31B , Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini Version (quant) UD-Q4_K_M or Q4_K_S Context size 16K-32K Cards at this size RTX 3090 , RTX 4090 , RX 7900 XTX , RTX PRO 4000 Extra Large VRAM 32 GB+ Models to try Qwen3.8-27B , Inkling 2 Mini Version (quant) UD-Q4_K_XL or Q6_K Context size 64K-128K+ Cards at this size RTX 5090 32GB , RTX PRO 4500 32GB , RTX PRO 5000 48GB , RTX PRO 6000 96GB Models marked MoE ( mixture of experts ) only run a few billion of their parameters for each token. They keep a decent speed on a smaller card with the rest held in system RAM, which is why a 35B model sits in the 16 GB row. On an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, our calculator puts Qwen3.6-35B at about 47 tokens per second this way. Feel free to experiment with several models until you find one that fits your needs. You can also use GPUPartner's VRAM Calculator to get an estimate. Can You Run Inkling 2 on an RTX 5090? Inkling 2 Mini, yes. Inkling 2 Small, no. Inkling 2 Mini is the newest model in this size class. Thinking Machines Lab released it on November 17, 2026: 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support and a 1M-token context. Unsloth's recommended file, UD-Q4_K_XL, is 17.6 GB. That is within 0.1 GB of the Qwen3.8-27B file in this guide, so it sits on a 32GB card the same way and leaves about 14GB for context. Nothing else in this guide changes. Update Unsloth Desktop first, because Inkling 2 needs a recent build, then search for Inkling 2 Mini in the same drop-down in Step 2. Inkling 2 Mini Memory needed Fits entirely on 2-bit 10-11 GB 12 GB card 3-bit 13-15 GB 16 GB card 4-bit (recommended) 17-18 GB 24 GB card 8-bit (lossless) 24 GB 32 GB card 2-bit Memory needed 10-11 GB Fits entirely on 12 GB card 3-bit Memory needed 13-15 GB Fits entirely on 16 GB card 4-bit (recommended) Memory needed 17-18 GB Fits entirely on 24 GB card 8-bit (lossless) Memory needed 24 GB Fits entirely on 32 GB card Those figures are Unsloth's. They count RAM and VRAM together and cover the model alone, so a long context needs more. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 5.4B parameters active, so the 4-bit file also runs on a 16 GB card with the remainder in system RAM, a little slower. Inkling 2 Small is small in name only. It is a 594B model, and the smallest file Unsloth publishes is 171.7 GB. That is unified-memory territory: a 256GB Mac Studio or a DGX Station , not a graphics card. Can You Run a Local AI on a Mac? Yes. You'll find good alternatives in Apple's Mac lineup thanks to its unified memory . Macs are pretty good at running larger models, even if they don't offer the best performance. Just make sure you grab the MLX flavor that is custom-built for Apple Silicon. The same trade applies to unified-memory PCs like the MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ 11M and NVIDIA's DGX Spark . How Do You Set Up a Local AI with Unsloth Desktop? It takes three steps: install Unsloth Desktop, download your model, and set the context size. I'll go over these steps in more detail below so you can follow along. Step 1: Install Unsloth Desktop First, we'll need a solution that 'serves' the AI model to you. My pursuit of simplicity narrowed my choices down to LM Studio or Unsloth Desktop. Both abstract away a ton of terminal commands and handle Python environments and dependencies behind a nice, simple UI, which makes them excellent picks for a first home setup. I landed on Unsloth Desktop mostly because, well, I liked the name better. Also, it didn't try to push the very thing I was trying to escape when I opened its website: a subscription. The community seems to like it overall too, so that's another point in its favor. Once you've clicked through the installer and launched Unsloth, you'll see a window like this one. Unsloth Desktop on first launch, before any model is loaded. Step 2: Download a Quantized Model On the top left of this main window, you can pick the model that you want to use from the drop down. We'll be using Qwen3.8-27B. The model picker. Qwen3.8-27B is first on the Recommended list. You should see a submenu like the one below when you click on a model. I'll be using Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL version. The M and S versions are smaller, but the XL version behaves much closer to the full-size model without filling up our VRAM, so it seemed like a good pick for my GPU. Every quantization of Qwen3.8-27B with its download size. The gear next to the downloaded one holds the context setting. Step 3: Set the Context Size Once the download completes, you should see a gear icon to the right of the model as shown in the screenshot above. Here, you can set your context size manually or leave it on Auto if you aren't sure how much you need. I'll be setting mine to 128K (unquantized) and might reassess after I've run the model through a few of my routine tasks for a few weeks. Again, you can use this VRAM calculator to help you with these numbers for your specific GPU . At this point, our first local AI is up and running, and you can start chatting with it right inside Unsloth. Remember, your mileage may vary depending on your setup. How Do You Share a Local AI Across Your Home Network? Short answer: Unsloth Desktop has LAN sharing built in. Set a Remote password, start LAN access, and share the address it gives you with anyone on your home network. Once Unsloth Desktop is set up with a model, you might want to give family members or friends access too. For now, we'll only serve it over our local network, so my family can use it without needing physical access to this PC. Head into Unsloth Desktop settings (gear icon on bottom left), and look for the 'Remote & LAN' tab. Settings, Remote & LAN. LAN access is the second card. The Remote access card above it is for a later part. Most of this section will be greyed out until you set a Remote password. Once you've set a password, you'll see a 'Start' button for LAN access. Click that and you should see an address that anyone on your home network can open in a browser to use a local AI model within a chat interface. They'll sign in as 'unsloth' with the Remote password you set. Just keep in mind that the PC needs to stay on with Unsloth running for anyone to reach it. Can You Access Your Local AI Across the Internet? Soon™ Not with this setup alone. Everything so far is limited to your local home network. If you just need a chat interface like ChatGPT, Gemini, etc. to work within your home network, you're basically done at this point! You and anyone on your network can start talking to an AI model hosted on your machine right away. In the next parts, we'll cover performance, tunneling, as well as setting up an agent that runs locally and uses only the web tools you allow it to use. This will let you automate more complex tasks like coding, research, and so much more without being tied to a subscription or usage limits and censorship. As always, my focus remains simplicity that allows my family to use it without too much guidance or help. PS. If you have any recommendations for agentic harnesses or even models to try, feel free to let me know and I'll give them a go!
