Dismiss alert {{ message }} AFK-surf xnulinux Repository navigation Code Issues 5 ( 5 ) Pull requests 4 ( 4 ) Actions Projects Security and quality Insights More items xnulinux Public Notifications You must be signed in to change notification settings Fork 160 ( 160 ) Star 3.5k ( 3.5k ) You must be signed in to star a repository About XNU as a loadable kernel module inside Linux (macOS personality for arm64 Linux) Resources Readme License Activity Custom properties Stars 3.5k stars Watchers 20 watching Forks 160 forks Report repository main Branches Tags Go to file Code Open more actions menu Latest commit History 269 Commits 269 Commits Folders and files Name Name Last commit message Last commit date .github/ workflows .github/ workflows LICENSES LICENSES docs docs fki-ko fki-ko gpu gpu kexts kexts linux linux scripts scripts tests/ host tests/ host tools tools xnu-ko xnu-ko xnu-patches xnu-patches LICENSE LICENSE README.md README.md View all files Repository files navigation README License More items xnulinux Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it. xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel module ( xnu.ko ) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module ( fki.ko ). With a stock Ubuntu kernel, insmod xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome. One system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 ( sw_vers , the Darwin kernel, launchd, WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu, Linux 7.0, the xnu and fki modules loaded, and the insmod xnu.ko process the macOS kernel runs in). Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800. The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge). Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on ( GPU=auto ). Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia ): hosted macOS 27 running with 4 CPUs and 8 GiB of RAM (CPU rendering), shown over macOS Screen Sharing alongside an SSH session from the DGX Spark host into the hosted Darwin userspace. Inside the hosted macOS on DGX Spark: About This Mac ( Chip: Unknown , 7.80 GB memory, macOS Golden Gate 27.2 ) alongside sysctl machdep.cpu ( ARM processor , hw.cpufamily: 0 , hw.ncpu: 4 ) and hw.optional.arm . How it works macOS processes (launchd, WindowServer, Safari...) Linux processes (systemd, sshd, xnudrmd...) ────────────────────────────────────────────────── ──────────────────────────────────────────── XNU (source-built, LINUX64 machine layer, kexts) │ ↕ linux64 host calls (xnu-patches/include/linux64_abi.h) xnu.ko (APSL side: loads and runs the kernel collection) ↕ FKI, the foreign kernel interface (fki_*) fki.ko (GPL side: CPUs, memory, faults, IPIs, files, network, host calls) Linux kernel (stock distro kernel, 4K pages, PAC) CPUs : each hosted CPU is a Linux kernel thread pinned to a Linux CPU. XNU runs on it until it calls the host (idle, I/O, a timer); Linux keeps its own exception vectors, and fki.ko forwards the faults and user exceptions of XNU code to XNU's handlers. Memory : XNU gets one physically contiguous block from Linux (CMA) and manages it with its own pmap; XNU and Linux share the user half of the address space layout (4K pages). Devices : kexts in kexts/ give macOS a disk (a file on the Linux side), a display (a framebuffer Linux reads), a keyboard and pointer, an Ethernet link (a Linux network interface), a keystore and a GPU bridge. GPU : Metal in the hosted macOS runs on gpu/xnu-cpu-metal (metal2vulkan over Vulkan). Vulkan reaches the Linux host's GPU through the DRM bridge ( kexts/XnuDrm → host call → gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd → the Linux render node), using Mesa's Venus driver; without a supported DRM bridge backend it falls back to Mesa lavapipe on the CPU. Status Working on two arm64 Linux setups: Apple Silicon Mac in an arm64 Linux VM ( krunkit , 1 to 6 hosted CPUs) : macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop with auto-login in 31–48 s (an Apple Virtualization macOS VM on the same Mac: 49 s). Apps open and quit, Spotlight and the file system work; a 30-minute stress run (40 rounds of Safari, Notes, Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings, Spotlight and a disk walk) finishes with no panic and no crash report. Runs as a systemd service: started at boot, stopped cleanly with the VM, restarted after a hosted-kernel panic, each run's log kept in /var/log/xnulinux/ . The GPU bridge gives hosted apps the host GPU ( Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max) ) and is enabled by default ( GPU=auto ) when a virtio-gpu render node is present, falling back to CPU rendering ( GPU=off ) otherwise. Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia ) : Boots to the full macOS desktop (Screen Sharing and SSH working) directly on bare-metal arm64 Linux with CPUS=4 and 8 GiB of RAM reserved for XNU. Currently renders on the CPU (Mesa lavapipe, GPU=off ): xnudrmd only forwards virtio-gpu (Venus) ioctls today, so hardware GPU pass-through on the GB10 GPU requires a new DRM bridge backend. Shipping it as a hosted service (what is distributed, what a user installs to run Apple's macOS) is in docs/hosted-service.md . What is still a stopgap is listed in docs/production.md . Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K). Requirements An arm64 Linux host with PAC ( FEAT_PAuth ), 4K pages, and at least 16 GB of RAM (8 GB reserved for the hosted kernel). Tested on: NVIDIA DGX Spark (bare-metal Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia ; CPU rendering for now). Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or later) running an arm64 Linux VM ( krunkit for GPU access via virtio-gpu Venus, or tart ). A Mac with Xcode to make the system disk and build the GPU parts. A macOS 27 installation (an Apple Virtualization VM disk) of your own. No Apple binaries are in this repository or distributed by it : the kexts Apple ships, the macOS system disk and its trust cache come from your own installation. Building and running scripts/vm-xnu-build.sh (on the arm64 Linux host, once): sets up the macOS-DroidVM Linux toolchain and builds XNU ( xnu-12377.121.6 ) natively on arm64. scripts/vm-xnu-rebuild.sh : applies xnu-patches/ , builds the kernel and kexts/ , and links the kernel collection with Apple's kexts from your macOS installation ( scripts/kclink ). To link that collection without building anything, scripts/apple-kc/link.sh , on the machine that runs xnu.ko , takes a kit of the built kernel and kexts and macOS 27.2's kernelcache, read from Apple's IPSW ( docs/free-kc.md ). scripts/mk-macvm-disk.sh (on the Mac): turns a macOS VM disk made by Apple's installer into the hosted system's disk and copies it into the Linux VM. scripts/xnulinux-boot.sh (on the arm64 Linux host): builds fki.ko and xnu.ko against the running kernel, brings up the network (and the GPU bridge when there is a render node) and boots the hosted system. Its console is scripts/xnu-console.sh , its screen tools/hosted/fb2png.py , input tools/hosted/xnu-input.py . On a bare-metal host (such as a DGX Spark), set the carve-out ( mem= , carve_base= , carve_mb= ) to fit the machine's physical memory layout, and set GPU=off ( xnudrmd supports only virtio-gpu for now). scripts/install-service.sh (on the arm64 Linux host): runs it as xnulinux.service , configured in /etc/xnulinux.conf (CPUs, memory, disk, GPU). On the Mac, scripts/install-krun-agent.sh keeps the VM itself running. GPU (optional, on the Mac): gpu/venus/build-darwin.sh builds the hosted Vulkan driver, gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/ the Metal plugin (see its README). Repository layout and licenses The Linux side and the XNU side are kept apart by license and meet only at FKI. Every source file carries an SPDX-License-Identifier ; the license texts are in LICENSES/ . Path License What fki-ko/ , linux/ GPL-2.0-only FKI: the out-of-tree module for stock kernels, and the same as an in-tree driver xnu-ko/ APSL-2.0 xnu.ko : loads XNU's kernel collection and runs it; calls Linux only through fki_* xnu-patches/ APSL-2.0 The LINUX64 machine layer and the other changes to XNU's sources, and their shared headers kexts/ APSL-2.0 The hosted system's kexts (CPU, disk, keystore, Metal accelerator, DRM bridge) kexts/XnuDisplay/ , kexts/XnuEthernet/ , kexts/XnuInput/ BSD-2-Clause-Patent Derived from macOS-DroidVM 's kexts gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/ GPL-2.0-or-later The Metal plugin over metal2vulkan (GPL-2.0-or-later); XnuCpuMetalShim.h is BSD-2-Clause-Patent (from AdrenoMetal ) gpu/xnu-drm/ GPL-2.0-only, MIT xnudrmd (the Linux end of the DRM bridge) is GPL; the protocol header and darwin/ (built into Mesa) are MIT gpu/venus/ GPL-2.0-only; patches MIT Build scripts and tests; the patches to Mesa and virglrenderer are under their upstream license (MIT) gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/patches/ upstream's Patches to Mesa (MIT) and metal2vulkan (GPL-2.0-or-later) scripts/ , tools/ , tests/ , docs/ GPL-2.0-only Build, disk, boot, debugging and test tools; documentation xnu.ko is on the XNU side of the line: it runs XNU's code in its own address space, so it is APSL-2.0 like XNU, and Linux reports it as a non-GPL module ( MODULE_LICENSE("Proprietary") , which taints the kernel as ZFS does). It must not include Linux headers beyond the module ABI, call Linux functions other than fki_* , or carry Linux code. Upstream code (XNU, macOS-DroidVM's toolchain, Mesa, metal2vulkan, the Vulkan loader, LLVM) is fetched at pinned revisions and patched at build time; it is never committed. Your trackpad will still talk. There's no speaker in a MacBook trackpad, just a small haptic motor that taps the glass so you feel a click. NO SPEAKER drives that motor up to 4,000 times a second, fast enough to make sound you can hear, and turns it into a voice. It talks, sings, raps, and becomes an instrument under your finger. One command. About a minute and a half. No speakers used. Watch the demo on X , with the sound on. 01 / before you start [ mute your mac ] it still talks; that's the point [ put it on a table ] on your lap it's much quieter [ hands off the glass ] until it asks you to touch it Space skips a part. q or Ctrl-C goes to the end. 02 / run it [ one line ] curl -fsSL a90.com/nospeaker | sh Downloads the latest release to ~/.local/bin/nospeaker and starts the show. a90.com/nospeaker points to play.sh in this repo, so you can read what it runs first. [ download ] Grab nospeaker.zip from the latest release , unzip it and run ./nospeaker in Terminal. Signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple. [ from source ] Needs Xcode or the Command Line Tools ( xcode-select --install ). Builds one program for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs. Built with only the Command Line Tools, the Intel part needs macOS 13 or later. git clone https://github.com/os6/nospeaker cd nospeaker ./build.sh ./nospeaker 03 / play with it ./nospeaker "hello there" say anything ./nospeaker --voice Daniel "hello" in another macOS voice ./nospeaker --sweep a rising tone, 100 Hz to 4 kHz --dark white on black --plain no visuals, plain text --external play through an external Magic Trackpad 04 / needs A Force Touch trackpad (built into MacBooks from 2015 on, or a Magic Trackpad 2 or newer), and macOS 12 or later. Without a Force Touch trackpad, it says so and exits. tested on MacBook Pro (Mac17,10) M5 Max macOS 27.2.1 everything works MacBook Pro (MacBookPro15,1) Intel macOS 15.7.4 works, built from source Not tested yet: a Magic Trackpad, and versions of macOS older than 15. MultitouchSupport is private, so older systems may lack the functions it uses, and loudness differs between trackpads. If you try it on another Mac, open an issue with your model, your macOS version and how it sounded. 05 / how it works say ──▶ formants ──▶ two tones ──▶ motor ──▶ glass per 10 ms F1 + F2 haptics sound Why you can hear it. The trackpad has no speaker, but the motor moves the glass. Driven back and forth hundreds or thousands of times a second, the glass vibrates fast enough to make sound you can hear. It's quiet because the motor is built for short taps, not for sound. The motor. MultitouchSupport is the private framework macOS uses for the trackpad. Its function MTActuationCreateFromDictionary takes a description of a vibration, a list of sine tones with a frequency, a strength and a length each, and MTActuationActuate plays it on the motor. Apple's public haptics API only offers three fixed taps. The range. Measured with the MacBook's own microphone, every semitone from 98 Hz to 3,951 Hz: how loud it is over a quiet room, and how much of the sound is the note itself. │ ### │ #+# +++##### # │ +#+#+ .+++##### .# │ . ++++#+#+ .+++##### # #.# # │ ++ +. . #..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+ #####.### .# │ +++#. +...+#..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+ #####.####+ .# │ ++++#... +...+#..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+.#####.####+ .# │ .++++#...++++...+#..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+.#####.####+ +# .# │..++++#...++++...+#..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+.#####.####+#.+# .#.# │..++++#...++++...+#..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+.#####.####+#.+#+..#.# └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 131 262 523 1047 2093 3951 public notes stop at 600 Hz ─┘ across: every semitone, in Hz · up: loudness, +16 to +34 dB # clean note + fair . mostly buzz It's loud from about 100 Hz to 4 kHz, with a few dead spots where the glass resonates. Its loudest, cleanest notes are around 1 kHz, which covers the most important part of a voice. The voice. macOS's own voice speaks the line into memory. Every 10 ms, linear prediction finds the voice's two strongest resonances (formants), its loudness and its pitch. The motor plays those two resonances as tones, restarted on every beat of the pitch, so they buzz like a voice instead of whistling. Hiss sounds (s, f, t) become quick bursts of high tones. Two resonances beat three: in a blind test they were clearer, and louder, because the motor's strength is split fewer ways. It sounds robotic, and it's much easier to follow when you can read along, which is why the show types every line as it speaks. The code. One Swift file, nospeaker.swift , with no dependencies. 06 / caveats Is it safe? It never drives the motor past its normal maximum strength. Going past it is possible and louder, but the driver starts to stall, so nospeaker doesn't. MultitouchSupport is private and undocumented, so a macOS update could break this. The MultitouchSupport function names were learned from the open-source Tactile project. Everything else was measured on a MacBook. ────────────────────── thanks for listening ─────────────────────── Made by Cody Collier · a90.com · MIT license About make your macbook's trackpad talk using its haptic motor x.com/codycollier Topics haptics macos swift trackpad Resources Readme MIT license Activity Stars 1.8k stars Watchers 2 watching Forks 91 forks Report repository Releases Packages Contributors Languages Footer © 2026 GitHub, Inc. Perplexity and Intelligence
body_text: Perplexity and Intelligence | OpenAI Skip to main content Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Log in Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Login OpenAI November 22, 2026 Research Safety Perplexity and Intelligence By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI Share From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently ⁠ (opens in a new window) , predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1 I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared ⁠ (opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts. A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “ an alien mind ⁠ ”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation. The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2 , 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5. The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets 4 , GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric. As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative. A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining. We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements 5 . While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining. Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation ⁠ (opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits , based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development. Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges: Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models. Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities. Not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities. Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence. At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry. Compute Scaling Ethics & Safety 2026 Author Jakub Pachocki Footnotes 1 It’s important to note that “compressor” in this sense is something that is capable of performing compression by predicting unseen data, not a compressed artifact like a GZIP file - that is, the best compressor trained on a given corpus does not necessarily “remember” the contents of the corpus. 2 In practice, we generally track the log of perplexity, also called cross-entropy loss . 3 The primary held-out datasets we’ve been using since GPT-3.5 are sourced from our internal codebase, and those are the numbers reported here (for a fixed snapshot). 4 Given what GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 were trained on, how well they predict code is a poor proxy for their general capabilities. This showcases a potential challenge arising from dataset selection with using perplexity as a shared metric; however it should still be informative to evaluate them jointly with modern models on general text. I chose to report perplexity on our internal codebase because I wanted to share the numbers we rely on most today to gauge progress in pretraining at OpenAI. 5 On the plot of losses of OpenAI models, you can see a steep acceleration in 2026. We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI ⁠ . An unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the service and installed malware on some of those devices. We blocked the identified attack path on November 20 and released security firmware that disables the known malware and removes the related files and traces identified during our investigation. We have submitted CVE reports for the vulnerabilities identified during our investigation into the attack and malware; CVE identifiers are pending. See technical details. Who is affected Receiving this notice, seeing an update prompt, or finding your model in the download tables does not mean your device was accessed. This incident involved devices connected to GoodCloud; a connection alone does not establish that an attack occurred. Your situation What it means and what to do Your device never connected to GoodCloud It was not likely exposed through this incident's attack path. Update the firmware as routine security maintenance. This incident alone is not a reason to reset the device or replace passwords and keys. Your device connected to GoodCloud, but you have no evidence of unauthorized access It may have been exposed, but compromise is not confirmed. Install the security firmware and follow the precautionary password and key guidance below. GL.iNet identified your device as affected, or you have evidence or a reasonable suspicion of unauthorized access Follow the recovery guidance below. If access appears to be ongoing, contain it first. For an affected KVM, also check the connected computer as a precaution. Some KVM devices have cloud service enabled before account linking. Not having a cloud account, or not linking a device, is not by itself proof that it never connected. See the KVM cloud-service documentation . If you are unsure about the device's connection history or a suspicious change, contact Support for help assessing it. What you should do now For all users: install the security firmware Install the latest stable security firmware for your exact model , using the official links below. You can update through the device's administration page; you do not need to run terminal commands or a security check first. Follow the router upgrade guide or KVM upgrade guide . An update is a preventive step for users without evidence of compromise. An update prompt alone does not require a reset or password changes. If you want an optional check or need to preserve evidence, do that before restarting, resetting, or updating, since those actions can remove signs of earlier activity. If unauthorized access is known or suspected: contain and recover If access appears to be ongoing, disconnect the device from the internet if you can do so safely and contact Support from another device. If disconnecting would cut off your only remote access, contact Support to plan recovery. For the strongest standard recovery assurance, download the official security firmware, install it without keeping settings, and manually configure the device again. Use new passwords and keys, and do not restore a backup from a potentially compromised device. On routers, turn Keep Settings off; on KVMs that offer it, clear Save current configuration . The upgrade guides above explain these options. If your model's options differ, ask Support for the appropriate procedure. A factory reset alone does not install the security fixes. Keeping settings remains an option you may choose , including to preserve remote access. The update still provides targeted cleanup for the known November 20 malware and can substantially reduce the risk from that malware. However, it may retain other unauthorized changes, so it provides less recovery assurance than reinstalling without settings. Contact Support if you need help choosing an approach or suspicious activity continues. For an affected KVM, also check the attached computer for unfamiliar accounts, software, browser extensions, startup items, or unexpected settings changes, and run a full scan with current security software. This is a precaution; it does not mean the attached computer was also accessed. See the KVM guidance in the incident announcement . If your device connected to GoodCloud: replace potentially exposed passwords and keys After updating or recovering the device, change passwords and replace access keys stored on or accessible from the GL.iNet device as a precaution, even if a check finds nothing. Examples include its administrator password and, if used, VPN and SSH keys. This advice does not mean every connected device was accessed or every password was copied. An update cannot revoke a key or password that was already copied. For other computers and devices, replace credentials if they were also stored on the GL.iNet device, reused there, or there is evidence or a reasonable suspicion that the other device was accessed. Simply connecting a computer by Ethernet or Wi-Fi does not, by itself, establish that its passwords were exposed. If you are unsure which credentials need changing, ask Support. The technical discussion of credential exposure explains why these precautions matter after unauthorized administrator access. Download and install the security update The security firmware disables the known malware from this incident and removes its related files and the traces identified during our investigation , including when settings are retained. It provides targeted cleanup; it is not a general malware scan or a complete integrity check. Additional vulnerability fixes and their cloud or firmware coverage are explained in Technical details and investigation findings . The cloud-side fix blocked the identified attack path, while firmware cleanup addresses the known malware already on a device. Neither can undo past access or revoke copied credentials. Follow the recovery guidance above if access is known or suspected. These tables list models with published security firmware, not confirmed compromised models. Install the latest stable release for your exact model; the versions below are the minimum security versions listed in this notice. If you installed a security beta, move to the latest stable release. Router security firmware downloads Model Minimum security version GL-MG1300 , GL-MT3000 , GL-MT6000 4.11.1 GL-E5800 4.10.3 GL-BE3600 , GL-BE9300 4.10.2 GL-BE14000 4.9.3 GL-BE6500 , GL-MT3600BE , GL-MT5000 4.9.1 GL-BE10000 4.8.7 GL-AX1800 , GL-AXT1800 , GL-SFT1200 , GL-X3000 , GL-XE3000 4.8.4 GL-MT2500 / GL-MT2500A , GL-X2000 4.7.14 GL-AXT1800: Install the security build from the official link above. If your device already shows 4.8.4 and you are unsure which build is installed, contact Support . KVM security firmware downloads Model Minimum security version RM1 , RM1V2 , RM10 , RM10RC , RM1PE , RM4PE 1.10.3 RMQ1 1.8.7 If your model is not listed, check the GL.iNet Download Center or ask Support which update applies. Do not install another model's firmware. The table is an update list, not a determination of which individual devices were affected. Optional device checks before updating Updating is the primary action. A check is optional and is not a prerequisite for installing the security firmware. If you want to check first, do so before restarting, resetting, or updating. Neither method below can rule out previous access or certify that a device is free of compromise. First choice for broader coverage: community security check The independently maintained community security check examines files, startup entries, running processes, and network connections for a broader set of known indicators. It can also flag indicators of the separate router persistence finding described below. This is an independent third-party project. Review its instructions and source code , and use check-only mode. Administrator access is required. Skip evidence collection, cleanup, and report submission if you only want to check. An unfamiliar change flagged for review is not automatically proof of infection. You may ask Support for help instead of running a script. Optional KVM check — limited coverage See the KVM quick-check instructions on the GL.iNet forum . A negative result does not rule out compromise; follow this bulletin's firmware and recovery guidance. Technical details and investigation findings How the incident happened GoodCloud's MQTT device-messaging service, deployed using EMQX, had a configuration error in message authorization. A client could send management messages to other users' connected devices without the required permission. This is a finding about GL.iNet's GoodCloud deployment , not a claim that every EMQX installation is vulnerable. The GoodCloud report describes the service-side authorization problem. A separate AstroWarp/SD-WAN input-handling flaw could cause management input to be executed as commands with root (administrator) privileges on affected routers, even when AstroWarp was turned off. A community report documents unauthorized remote command access on a GoodCloud-connected router. The RTTY finding below concerns remote-terminal connection security. These are distinct issues; the router command-injection flaw should not be assumed to explain every KVM compromise. Vulnerability reports and remediation coverage The links below point to GL.iNet's published vulnerability reports. Official CVE identifiers remain subject to assignment/publication confirmation ; report titles and internal tracking references are not CVE numbers. Vulnerability report Security impact Remediation and firmware coverage GoodCloud message authorization — GitHub report Unauthorized messages could change device configuration or invoke device management APIs. Further impact depends on what the device accepts and processes. The report identifies GoodCloud v3.19.13 as affected and v3.19.14 as fixed. The identified cloud attack path was blocked on November 20. This is a service-side fix; device firmware separately provides incident malware cleanup. AstroWarp/SD-WAN command injection — GitHub report Insufficient input validation could allow root command execution on the listed routers, including with AstroWarp disabled. The report lists model-specific expected fix versions. The download tables above identify published incident security releases; check the exact model and build. The report's planned-version wording alone does not verify every shipped build. This router finding is not a KVM vulnerability claim. RTTY configuration and TLS certificate verification — GitHub report If relevant startup arguments can be modified, intended server-certificate verification can be bypassed, allowing connection to an attacker-controlled terminal server and root access. The report identifies 1.10.3 as fixed for RM1, RM10, RM10RC, RM1PE, RM1V2, and RM4PE, and 1.8.7 for RMQ1. Its router entries use expected fix wording; those entries do not by themselves confirm publication or verification of every planned router fix. Fixing a vulnerability and cleaning up a compromised device are different tasks. The versions above describe the linked reports' remediation status; they are not a finding that every listed device was attacked. Retained settings, copied credentials, and changes outside the targeted cleanup can still require recovery action. Additional findings and recovery limits Separate router persistence reports. Community users reported a modified startup script and suspicious processes; GL.iNet acknowledged these reports in the forum . Some reported file dates predate November 20. The original reports do not establish the initial entry path or a connection to this incident. A process name alone is not proof of infection. Do not assume incident malware cleanup resolves every separate persistence finding. Why keeping settings can leave other changes. Community KVM testing reported that an added startup script and SSH key survived a configuration-preserving upgrade on a test RM1. This illustrates a recovery limit; it does not establish that every affected KVM had those modifications. For known or suspected compromise, reinstall without keeping configuration using the model's supported upgrade options. Firmware and boot integrity. Community recovery analysis explains that a normal reset or firmware reinstall may not rewrite every flash region. This is a recovery limitation, not evidence that boot components were changed in this attack. Contact Support if there are reasons to suspect deeper changes or activity persists after recovery. Other devices and credentials. We have not confirmed access to other devices through a compromised GL.iNet device. However, root access can expose credentials held on that device, as explained in the remote-access case report . Not confirming access to another device does not eliminate that credential risk. Investigation and further updates Security firmware has already been released for the models listed above. Its availability does not mean every device of those models was compromised, and additional findings do not establish that all listed devices share the same vulnerabilities. We are continuing to determine the number of affected devices, the timeline of unauthorized activity, and whether computers connected to affected KVMs were accessed. As individual findings are verified, we will update this notice and publish model-specific advisories identifying the relevant versions, confirmed fixes, and any further actions. Any additional firmware work will be described separately from the security releases already available. Our commitment to customers We’re sorry for the concern and disruption this incident caused. Updating and recovering devices takes time, especially when they are managed remotely. Our Support team is ready to help you assess your device, choose a recovery approach, and interpret check results. Teams across GL.iNet are continuing the investigation and adding safeguards to our cloud services and device firmware. We will share confirmed findings and further guidance as they become available. Frequently asked questions 1. Was my device affected by this incident? Devices that never connected to GoodCloud were not exposed through this incident's attack path. Devices that connected could have been exposed, but connection alone does not establish compromise. AstroWarp being turned off does not rule out GoodCloud exposure. Some KVMs can connect before account linking. If your connection history is unclear, contact Support. Keep firmware up to date as routine security maintenance. 2. Does a check that finds nothing mean my device was unaffected? No. A check covers only the indicators it looks for, and restarting or updating can remove signs. Install the security firmware regardless of the result. For optional checks, use the community check for routers or broader KVM coverage. The short KVM check has limited coverage. 3. Who needs to change passwords and keys or check other devices? For devices that connected to GoodCloud, and for any device you know or suspect was compromised, replace credentials stored on or accessible from the device after updating or recovery. This is a precaution even without a positive check. A device that never connected and has no other reason to suspect compromise does not need incident-related credential replacement. Check the computer attached to an affected KVM; for other devices, use the exposure and access criteria in What you should do now . 4. Can the same GoodCloud attack path still be used? We blocked the identified attack path on November 20. That service-side fix does not remove malware already installed on a device. Install the security firmware and follow the recovery guidance appropriate to your situation. The vulnerability reports above describe the scope of each fix. 5. Will I receive an email if my device was affected? We will email customers whose devices we identify as affected using the address associated with their GL.iNet cloud account, including when a device has since been rebooted or updated. Not receiving an email is not proof that a device was unaffected. Do not wait for a notification before installing the security firmware or seeking help if you suspect compromise. 6. Do I need to factory reset or reinstall firmware? An update prompt alone is not a reason to reset. If unauthorized access is known or suspected, the strongest standard recovery option is to reinstall official security firmware without preserving settings, then manually configure the device again. Turn off Keep Settings on a router or Save current configuration on a supported KVM upgrade. Keeping settings remains your choice, with the cleanup limits explained above. A reset alone does not install the fixes. See the linked upgrade guides or ask Support about your model. Contact For device checks, firmware updates, and recovery, email support@gl-inet.com . To report a security issue, email security@gl-inet.com . Update history November 20, 2026 (UTC): Initial notice issued. November 22, 2026 (UTC): Added the community security check and further information. November 23, 2026 (UTC): Updated with pending CVE reports(identifies pending assessment) and additional findings. title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
body_text: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis | Lean community blog Skip to main content Lean community blog Main site Archive Tags About RSS feed Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative 2026-11-21 13:55 Source Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Joint statement by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative. On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code. We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement. Our rationale is outlined below. The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied. The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory. Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures. The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools ( comparator and con-leche –compare ), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis. The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/ . These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources. Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification. We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof. Previous post Contents © 2026 The Lean prover community - Powered by Nikola

title: Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Max Tegmark
body_text: Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Top MIT Physicist | Novara Media Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Top MIT Physicist | Novara Media Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Top MIT Physicist Support Us NM About Support Newsletters Events How We Are Funded Merch Shop ➞ Manage Donation Shows Novara Live Downstream Interviews If I Speak… Do Your Own Research ACFM Series Death in Westminster Committed Foreign Agent Planet B Articles Latest Feature Analysis Opinion Report Long Read Red Flags Search this site News Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Top MIT Physicist Apparently they discuss overthrowing the US government after a few drinks. by Clare Hymer 24 November 2026 Novara Media Employees at US artificial intelligence company Anthropic openly talk about “overthrowing the US government” and “taking over the world”, a world-renowned physicist has claimed. In an interview with Novara Media , Max Tegmark, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said: “When I talk to people who work for Anthropic, after they’ve had a couple of drinks, the conversation often gets into overthrowing the US government and taking over the world.” “They tend to not use words like ‘coup’ and ‘overthrow the US government’. They instead use the code phrase ‘alignment without control’,” he said. ‘Alignment without control’ is the idea that AI should be kept in check by being instilled with certain values – likely those shared by Anthropic, Tegmark said – rather than being directly controlled by humans. “We get the sort of future that Alan Turing predicted, where it’s going to be Anthropic’s machine-god running Earth, and then the rest of us just have to hope that somehow it’s gonna be nice.” Turing, widely regarded as the founder of computer science, famously warned in 1951 that once machines started thinking, we should expect them to take control. Tegmark said the comments from Anthropic staff should alarm anyone who cares about democracy. “These companies really don’t seem to like it [democracy]. They have lobbied really hard to even prevent any meaningful government oversight of them,” he said. He added: “Here in the US, OpenAI and Anthropic are less regulated than a sandwich shop.” Novara Media has approached Anthropic for comment. Tegmark’s disclosure comes as protests against AI are ramping up across the world. As Anthropic started trading on the stock market at a staggering $2tn valuation on Thursday, protesters gathered at both the Nasdaq exchange in New York and the firm’s San Francisco headquarters demanding an AI development slowdown. On Saturday, over 1,000 people marched against “AI extinction” in London in what campaigners said was “the biggest AI safety march in history”. Clare Hymer is head of articles at Novara Media.
